The Art Director's Direction Manuals

One cover, many volumes. Each manual is a self-contained, zero-fluff breakdown you can hand to a stylist, a gaffer, or an agency — built around photographing women and women's products with light that flatters and respects. Written for photographers at any level and any camera — every recipe is body-agnostic, giving the lens focal length and settings, never a specific model.

Camera
Any ILC body
Lens
24–70mm f/2.8 or equiv.
Space
Any · studio or location
Volumes
108 live · complete

How to read this manual

Start here

New to lighting or just new to this genre? Start here. Every volume is a self-contained shoot recipe you can run on any interchangeable-lens camera — we give the lens focal length and the settings, never a specific body. The studio volumes assume a space you can darken and control with your own lights; the outdoor volumes use available daylight. Both adapt to any room, rented studio, or location — there is no fixed venue here. Work top to bottom, or jump to a volume from the contents.

Each volume gives you

  • A baseline rig — the light setup, stated once, that every look in the volume builds on.
  • Three looks — each with styling, a lighting micro-adjustment, and posing direction.
  • A top-down lighting plan — where every light, the subject and the camera sit.
  • Posing or camera-angle sketches — at portrait, half and full-body crops.
  • An on-set crew brief — separate instructions for the photographer, model, MUA and stylist.

Reading the lighting plan

  • Key light (softbox / octabox / dish)
  • Sun (outdoor volumes)
  • Negative fill — black card, subtracts light
  • Positive fill — white card, bounces light in
  • Rim / hair light

The ring is the subject (the small wedge shows the way they face); the trapezoid at the bottom is the camera.

New here? A path through the fundamentals

  1. One-Light Portrait — do everything with a single source
  2. The Clamshell — the flattering two-light beauty rig
  3. Rembrandt, Loop & Split — name and place the shadow
  4. The Butterfly — classic glamour light
  5. Backlight & Rim and Into Shadow — shape and mood
  6. Then a genre: Neutral Commercial, Clean Beauty, or Warm Authority

Glossary — the words in plain English

Key light
The main, brightest source that shapes the subject. Everything else is measured against it.
Fill
Light added back into the shadow side to soften contrast. More fill = brighter, gentler.
Negative fill
A black card or flag that subtracts light to deepen shadow and carve shape.
Rim / hair light
A light from behind that outlines the subject, separating them from the background.
Feather
Aiming a light so its soft edge — not its hot centre — lands on the subject. Softer, more even.
Ratio
The brightness gap between the lit and shadow sides, e.g. 2:1 (gentle) vs 8:1 (dramatic).
Aperture (f-stop)
Controls depth of field. A low number (f/2.8) blurs the background; a high one (f/11) keeps more sharp.
Focal length
How tight the lens frames, in mm. Longer (70mm+) flatters faces and compresses; wider (24mm) shows more.
Shutter speed
Controls motion. Fast (1/200) freezes; slow (1/15) blurs or drags. Strobe freezes by flash duration.
ISO
Sensor sensitivity. Keep it low (100) in the studio for the cleanest files; raise it in low light.
White balance (WB)
Keeps colours true. Lock it under mixed or gelled light so skin stays natural.
Clamshell
A soft key above plus a fill below — the flattering, near-shadowless beauty standard.
Backlight
Light placed behind the subject for glow, a rim, or (in food) freshness.
Golden hour
The warm hour after sunrise or before sunset — the flattering window for outdoor work.

Vol. 01 Model portfolio · Agency pitch

Noir Commercial

Pure presence over performance. The frame is carved, not filled — high contrast, structural posing, and strategic negative space, delivered through a dark, sophisticated lens.

IntermediateKit 1–2 lights + a modifier
Model portfolioAgency pitchStructureTailoringAuthorityTexture

RelatedThe Intimate · Neutral Commercial · Clean Beauty

Baseline rig — constant across all three looks

Key — Octabox

45° elevated, camera-left. Soft, directional core. The single source of shape; everything else subtracts.

Negative fill — Black V-flat

Shadow side, close. Subtracts ambient to carve the jawline and drive black-side contrast.

Rim — Striplight

3/4 back. A clean vertical edge for subject separation off a falling-to-black ground.

Capture

24–70mm · ISO 100 · 1/160 sync. Meter for highlight; let the shadows fall.

Starting exposureManual · 1/160 sync · f/8 · ISO 100 · WB 5200KShutter controls ambient only — flash power sets the exposure. Sync tops out near 1/200; switch to HSS for 1/250 and up.
01
Structure · Tailoring · Authority

The Architect

The power frame. Sharp tailoring read as silhouette — black-on-black separation that says the subject can carry a campaign.

Headshot
70mm · f/8
Three-quarter
35–40mm
Full length
24–28mm
Key move
Feather past face
Fill
Tighten to crush
A

Styling & Textures

Charcoal-to-ink worsted wool suiting, single-breasted, structured shoulder, sharp notch or peak lapel. High-twist, matte cloth only — dense wool and dry cotton hold shadow instead of throwing specular glare.

Under it, a bone-white cotton poplin shirt, collar open, no tie — or a slim black knit tie. Keep the whole look inside the black–graphite band; the shirt is the one controlled highlight anchor.

Ban list

No satin, sheen, or synthetics — they blow out under the octabox and cheapen the frame.

B

Lighting Micro-Adjustments

Feather the key: rotate the octabox so the beam core passes just past the face and the soft edge grazes it. Preserves shadow detail in the black cloth and keeps the wool matte.

Bring the V-flat in to ~30–45cm off the shadow cheek — deepen the jawline and let the suit's shadow side fall toward black to carve the outline.

Rim

Feather the striplight along the shoulder seam to trace the tailored line. Meter the shirt at f/8; let the rest go.

C

Posing Architecture & Micro-Expressions

Body: weight on the back foot, front foot light — a slight backward lean reads as authority. Drop and rotate the rear shoulder ~15° to open the lapel to the key. Chin down a touch, forehead toward camera. One thumb in the trouser pocket to break the mass.

Eyes: direct to lens, lids relaxed — never wide. Set focus on the far corner of the lens for a long, unbothered gaze.

Micro-expression

Jaw set, lips closed-neutral with the faintest downturn. Stoic — not a scowl.

02
Texture · Skin · Intimacy

The Skin

The beauty and grooming plate. Strip to the body and let raking light read skin and knit — the frame agencies check for range and honesty.

Beauty crop
70mm · f/5.6
Detail
70mm · min focus
Key move
Drop to ~30°
Fill
Add 2nd flag
Rim
Whisper only
A

Styling & Textures

Pull back to a ribbed or waffle-knit singlet in bone, ecru, or raw undyed cotton — or bare shoulders draped in heavy raw linen. Choose a textural knit (chunky rib, boucle) that catches the rake.

Hold everything warm-neutral: bone, ecru, tobacco, greige. Nothing competes with skin, which is now the primary texture.

Grooming

Matte the skin — powder the T-zone. Shine is the enemy of a clean skin book.

B

Lighting Micro-Adjustments

Commit to the rake: drop the key from 45° toward ~30° and feather hard so light skims the cheekbone and clavicle, maximising skin and knit texture.

Crush the fill: pull the V-flat closer and add a second black flag on the shadow side — one lit plane, one dying to black. A grid on the octabox keeps the ground falling off.

Rim

Ease the striplight down so separation is a whisper, not a graphic line. Intimacy over edge. Meter skin at f/5.6.

C

Posing Architecture & Micro-Expressions

Body: closer and quieter. Rotate the torso ~30° off-axis so one shoulder leads and the collarbone catches the rake; spine long, sternum barely lifted. Bring the chin forward and slightly down to lengthen the neck against the black fill. A hand to the collarbone or hairline adds tactile, editorial skin-on-skin.

Eyes: half-lidded, focus pulled ~30° off-lens for the introspective "caught" frames; then one set locked to lens, lips just parted.

Micro-expression

Vulnerability under control — breath held, not performed.

03
Drama · Silhouette · Negative Space

The Silhouette

The editorial statement. The garment's outline is the subject; the face need not always meet the lens. Two-thirds of the frame is deliberate black.

Full length
24–28mm · f/8
Movement
35mm · burst
Attitude
50mm waist-up
Key move
Raise & back off
Rim
Hero · +1
A

Styling & Textures

Long-line drama: a full-length black wool overcoat, or floor-grazing tailored trousers under an open robe-coat. Choose cloth with movement — heavyweight wool crepe, gabardine, matte technical drape — that holds an architectural line and swings on the walk.

All black, all matte. One structural accessory at most — a leather glove, a sharp boot. No jewellery glare.

Priority

Shape over texture. The silhouette is the product.

B

Lighting Micro-Adjustments

Widen the scene: raise and back the key off so it covers the full body evenly without a hot foreground; drop output and add distance to harden the shadow for a graphic edge.

Rim becomes hero: stand the striplight hard 3/4 back and vertical to trace the whole body edge — the only thing separating a black coat from a black ground. Reposition the V-flat to guard the figure's shadow edge.

Composition

Light one plane; let two-thirds fall to black. Meter for rim separation, body low-key at f/8.

C

Posing Architecture & Micro-Expressions

Body: full contrapposto — weight on one leg, opposite hip released, opposite shoulder counter-rotated into an S-line. Arms make angles, not curves: one elbow out to build a triangle of negative space. For movement, walk through slowly on burst and catch the coat at its apex.

Eyes: to lens, distant and unbothered — or turned to a fixed horizon on the profile frames, which reads as intention, not absence.

Micro-expression

A still, stoic mask. All the drama lives in the body and the cloth.

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Build a single hard key at 45 degrees with deep negative fill so shadows fall inky and graphic across her jaw and shoulder. Shoot tight, expose for the highlights, and let the background drop fully to black for that noir separation.

Model

Lead with slow, deliberate turns of the chin so we can carve the light along one cheekbone at a time. Hold a cool, self-possessed gaze just off-lens and let the stillness read as authority.

MUA & Hair

Matte the skin to kill any specular hotspots the hard key will exaggerate, and sculpt a defined brow and a deep matte lip. Keep hair sleek and controlled so no stray strands break the clean shadow line.

Stylist

Dress in structured black or charcoal with strong shoulders and clean tailoring that reads as silhouette against the dark field. Avoid busy texture or logos so the eye stays on face and form.

Pose & direction library
Poses & body
  1. Shoulder squared to a single hard key, face turned a quarter into shadow
  2. Chin dropped, eyes lifted so the catchlight sits high and bright
  3. Hand grazing the jaw, elbow anchored low to carve a lit triangle
  4. Back to camera, head rotated so only the lit cheek reads
  5. Seated, forearms on knees, spine curved forward into the beam
  6. Weight on the rear hip, front shoulder dipped away from the light
  7. One hand sliding into slicked hair, arm framing the dark side
  8. Leaning a shoulder on an unseen wall, half the body swallowed by black
  9. Collar popped and gripped, knuckles catching the sharp edge of key
  10. Profile pose, nose bridge riding the exact line between light and dark
Expression & mimic
  • Long slow exhale, lips just parted, no smile
  • Eyes narrowed a fraction as if reading someone across a room
  • Gaze cast down the barrel of the lens, unblinking on the frame
  • Micro-tension in the jaw, held for the beat before release
  • Look pulled hard off-camera into the shadow side
  • Half-lidded, breath settling, shoulders dropping on the cue
Directing cues
  • “Turn slow until you feel the light hit just one cheek — stop there.”
  • “Give me nothing. Let the shadow do the talking.”
  • “Breathe out, and on the empty lungs, look at me.”
  • “Think of a secret you’re not going to tell me.”
  • “Drop the chin a hair — there, now the eyes catch.”
  • “Hold it… hold it… and let the face go quiet.”
MUA & hair
  • Matte skin, zero shine on the shadow side to keep black true
  • Deep contour under the cheekbone to extend the carved plane
  • Slicked-back or wet-look hair to hold a clean lit edge
  • Defined brow and a bold matte lip, everything else restrained
  • Skip highlighter — let the single key make the only shine
On-set checklist

The pitch package

What leaves the studio, cut for how agencies actually read a new face — range proven across scale, mood, and body, with the through-line intact.

Range in three

Authority, skin, and drama — one board each, so a booker reads versatility in a single pass.

Focal spread

A confirmed headshot, three-quarter, and full-length from every look — 70mm compression through to 24mm architecture.

The through-line

One lighting philosophy across all three: carved, contrasted, deliberate. It signals a model who takes direction and holds a mood.

Retouch note

Protect texture. Keep skin and cloth honest — the noir contrast does the work; heavy retouching undoes it.

Vol. 02 Model portfolio · Commercial range

Neutral Commercial

The counterweight to the noir book. Clean, soft, and true-to-life — approachable presence that casts wide across lifestyle, e-commerce, and mainstream commercial, while staying high-end.

BeginnerKit 1–2 lights + a modifier
Model portfolioCommercial rangeClean tailoringApproachable authorityCasual knitNatural

Baseline rig — the noir setup, inverted

Key — Large Octabox

~30° elevated, close and more frontal. A soft wrap that flatters rather than carves — the modifier does the softening the negative fill used to fight.

Positive fill — White V-flat

Shadow side, bounced back in. Opens the ratio to a gentle 2:1 so shadows read as detail, not drama.

Background — Lit separately

Neutral seamless held at clean mid-grey to white. The rim retires; the bright ground does the separation.

Capture

24–70mm · ISO 100–200 · WB 5400K. True colour, f/5.6–8 for e-comm sharpness. Meter for even skin.

Starting exposureManual · 1/160 sync · f/8 · ISO 100 · WB 5200KShutter controls ambient only — flash power sets the exposure. Sync tops out near 1/200; switch to HSS for 1/250 and up.
01
Clean tailoring · Approachable authority

The Open

Trust before intimidation. Soft tailoring in daylight-clean light — the frame that lands corporate campaigns and premium lifestyle alike.

Headshot
70mm · f/8
Three-quarter
50mm
Full length
35mm

A

Styling & Textures

Soft, relaxed tailoring in stone, oat, and off-white — cotton, linen-wool, an unstructured shoulder and open collar. Light, matte naturals with gentle texture so the even light reads as quality cloth, not flatness.

Keep it tonal and warm-neutral head to toe. No hard black; the darkest note is a soft taupe.

Ban list

No stark white that clips, no busy pattern — clean light punishes both.

B

Lighting Micro-Adjustments

Centre the key: bring the octabox more frontal and closer for an even, flattering wrap — the opposite of feathering it away.

Swap subtract for add: replace the black V-flat with a white one and bounce fill back in until the shadow ratio sits near 2:1. Faces open, skin stays true.

Ground

Light the seamless to a clean mid-grey. Meter skin evenly at f/8 for catalogue-safe sharpness.

C

Posing Architecture & Micro-Expressions

Body: open and squared. Weight even or a gentle contrapposto, shoulders relaxed and level, chin held on the horizon. Hands easy — one loosely in a pocket, or arms uncrossed and forward. Nothing guarded.

Eyes: engaged straight to lens, focus on the near iris — bright, present, unforced.

Micro-expression

A warm micro-smile that lives in the eyes, lips barely closed. Approachable, credible, not toothy.

02
Casual knit · Natural · Lifestyle

The Daylight

The lifestyle plate. Window-soft light and relaxed styling — the frames brands buy for feeling human and in-the-moment.

Portrait
70mm · f/4
Candid
50mm
Key move
Big scrim, side
Fill
Wide bounce
Ratio
~3:2 airy
A

Styling & Textures

Casual and tactile: a soft chunky knit, washed denim, an easy tee in bright neutrals. Texture that reads warm — the raking softness catches loops and weave without hardening them.

Palette stays light and lived-in — cream, sky-washed blue, soft grey. Real, wearable, uncostumed.

Note

A touch of movement in the cloth sells "natural" — nothing pressed or stiff.

B

Lighting Micro-Adjustments

Mimic a window: push a large scrim or the octabox in tight from the side for soft directional daylight, and fill wide with a big bounce so the whole scene stays open and airy.

Lift the ratio to ~3:2 — the gentlest contrast in the book. Let the background go bright and clean behind.

Feel

Aim for light that looks found, not built. Nothing should read as "lit."

C

Posing Architecture & Micro-Expressions

Body: loose and in-motion. Natural gestures — a hand through the hair, a half-turn, weight shifting mid-step. Let the shoulders round slightly; ease, not architecture.

Eyes: soft and often off-camera to a natural eyeline, then a few genuine looks back to lens. Catch the frame between beats.

Micro-expression

A real, unforced laugh or exhale — the crinkle at the eyes is the shot.

03
Full body · Brand · Bright space

The Space

The e-commerce and brand plate. Even full-length coverage and bright negative space — clean enough to drop into any layout.

Full length
28–35mm · f/8

A

Styling & Textures

A complete, clean commercial look — considered lines, brand-ready neutral palette head to toe. Cloth that holds shape without drama: crisp cotton, fine knit, a tailored trouser with a clean break.

Everything tonal and layout-friendly — the garment must survive being cut out onto white.

Priority

Legibility of the full outfit over mood. This is the product page.

B

Lighting Micro-Adjustments

Even it out: broaden and raise the key for uniform full-body coverage, top to shoe, with fill on both sides so no limb falls dark. Control the floor shadow to a soft, single contact.

Bright negative space: keep the seamless high-key so the empty frame reads light and open — the inverse of the noir black void.

Ground

High-key, low contrast, true colour. Meter body and background within a stop.

C

Posing Architecture & Micro-Expressions

Body: clean commercial stance — a confident, grounded contrapposto that keeps the silhouette open and the outfit fully legible. Add a walking or gentle-motion set; angles stay relaxed, never severe.

Eyes: direct to lens, confident and friendly, focus on the near iris for the hero; easy off-lens looks for the motion frames.

Micro-expression

Assured and open — a poised half-smile that a broad brand can read as its own.

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Light soft and even with a large source and gentle fill so skin stays flattering and neutral for broad commercial use. Frame with generous negative space around her for later crop and copy placement.

Model

Keep expressions warm, open, and approachable, cycling through a small range of natural smiles and relaxed resting looks. Reset your posture between frames so nothing stiffens into a pose.

MUA & Hair

Deliver a clean, healthy no-makeup makeup with even tone and soft definition that photographs true across many uses. Style hair simple and tidy so it never dates the image or distracts from the message.

Stylist

Choose solid, muted separates in neutral tones that stay versatile and brand-safe. Steam every seam and pin the back so the fit reads crisp under flat light.

Pose & direction library
Poses & body
  1. Open stance, weight even, both shoulders squared to camera
  2. Relaxed contrapposto with hands loose at the sides

  8. Gentle S-curve through the spine, head returning to neutral
  9. Hands clasped low in front, elbows soft, no tension
  10. Three-quarter turn, glancing back over the near shoulder
Expression & mimic
  • Soft genuine smile that reaches the eyes
  • Relaxed neutral with the lips lightly together
  • Small laugh caught on the way down
  • Warm steady eye contact, brow at ease
  • Slow blink, then re-engage the lens
  • Easy exhale, shoulders releasing on the frame
Directing cues
  • “Shake out your hands, then let them land wherever feels natural.”
  • “Tell me what you had for breakfast — just talk to me.”
  • “Soft smile, like you just spotted a friend across the street.”
  • “Roll your shoulders back and down, then settle.”
  • “Look just past my ear, then bring your eyes to the lens.”
  • “Great — stay exactly there, that’s the one.”
MUA & hair
  • Natural skin-true base with light, even coverage
  • Cream blush for a healthy, believable flush

On-set checklist

The pitch package

The commercial counterpart to Vol. 01 — proof the same face casts warm and wide, not only dark. Pair the two books to show full tonal range in one submission.

Range in three

Authority, lifestyle, and brand — one board each, tuned for how commercial clients screen for likeability and fit.

Focal spread

A clean headshot, three-quarter, and full-length per look — 70mm portrait through to 28mm e-commerce.

The through-line

One soft, true-to-life philosophy across all three: even, flattering, honest colour. It signals a model who is easy to art-direct and easy to sell.

Retouch note

Keep it clean and natural. Even skin and true colour — resist over-smoothing; commercial buyers want believable.

Vol. 03 Still life · Product hero

Controlled Reflection

Precision over mood. Where the portrait volumes carve a person, this one shapes light on a surface — gradients, edges, and reflections placed by hand for a premium product hero.

IntermediateKit 2 lights + cards, tripod
Still lifeProduct heroMatte heroForm & edgeReflectiveLiquid

RelatedLingerie — Intimate Apparel · Glassware & Liquids — Refraction · Electronics & Tech — Clean Glow

Baseline rig — the still-life bench

Key — Large softbox / scrim

Overhead-side, feathered for a controlled gradient across the surface. Size and distance set the length of the highlight roll-off.

Shapers — White + black cards

The real tools. White cards fill and add highlights; black flags cut edges and define form on reflective bodies.

Surface — Acrylic / seamless

Black acrylic for reflection, seamless sweep for clean e-comm. A separately-graded background carries the gradient.

Capture

24–70mm · tripod · ISO 100 · f/11–16 with focus-stacking for edge-to-edge sharp. Tether and chimp reflections live.

Starting exposureManual · 1/160 · f/11–f/16 · ISO 100 · WB 5200K · tripodFocus-stack for front-to-back sharpness; tether and check reflections and label detail at 100% before you move on.
01
Matte hero · Form & edge

The Monolith

Packaging and matte goods. Directional light builds three-dimensional form; black flags carve the edges off the background.

Hero
50–70mm · f/13
Stack
6–10 frames
Key
Side, feathered
Shape
Black flags · edges
Ground
Graded gradient
A

Set & Surface

Product on a clean sweep or a matte tile that echoes the packaging's material story. Dress minimally — the object is the subject; any prop earns its place or leaves.

Background graded to a soft dark-to-light gradient behind the hero so the top edge catches light and the base grounds in shadow.

Prep

De-dust, fingerprint-check, and align labels dead-square before a frame is shot.

B

Lighting Micro-Adjustments

Rake for form: bring the softbox to the side and slightly back, feathered, so one face lights bright and the adjacent face falls to controlled shadow — the read that makes a box look solid.

Flag the edges: stand black cards close on the shadow side to snap the product's outline off the background. A white card opposite lifts the shadow just off black.

Highlight

Add a small striplight or silver card for a single controlled specular on the top edge — one accent, not many.

C

Composition & Camera

Angle: a high three-quarter shows two faces and the top — the classic hero that reads volume. Keep verticals true; correct any keystone in-camera or on the tether.

Focus: stack 6–10 frames at f/13 for front-to-back sharpness the crop can survive.

Frame

Leave clean negative space for layout copy — shoot to the brief's aspect, not just square.

02
Reflective · Liquid · Glass

The Liquid

Bottles, glass, and chrome. Here you light the reflections, not the object — a gradient scrim behind does most of the work.

Hero
70mm · f/14
Key
Scrim behind
Edges
Black cards
Highlight
Strip · controlled
Surface
Black acrylic
A

Set & Surface

Set on black acrylic for a clean mirror foot. Fill liquids to a consistent line; a hair of glycerin holds bubbles where you want them and kills them where you don't.

The set is mostly cards. The bottle reflects its whole surroundings, so build the environment the glass will show back.

Fingerprints

Gloves on. On glass, every touch is a two-hour retouch you can avoid.

B

Lighting Micro-Adjustments

Light the background, not the bottle: put a gradient scrim behind and let the glass transmit and refract it. That luminous core is the product, glowing from within.

Draw the edges: flank with black cards so the sides of the glass render as clean dark rails — definition on a transparent object comes from the darks, not the lights.

Label

A small dedicated source or card relights the label without flaring the shoulder of the bottle.

C

Composition & Camera

Angle: near eye-level to keep the liquid line honest and the label square. A whisper of downward tilt only if the cap needs to read.

Focus: stack through the depth of the glass; f/14 base. Shoot separate label and highlight passes to composite for a flawless hero.

Note

Judge reflections on the tether at 100% — the eye lies at bench distance.

03
Texture · Macro · Material

The Grain

Fabric, powder, food, raw material. Extreme raking light and macro turn surface into the story — the detail plate for a premium brand.

Macro
70mm · f/16
Stack
12–20 frames
Key
Extreme rake
Fill
Whisper white
Angle
Top-down flatlay
A

Set & Surface

Fill the frame with the material itself — weave, grain, powder, pile. Style it to look effortless but intentional: a fold, a drift, a scatter with a hero point of interest.

Neutral tonal ground so the texture, not the colour contrast, carries the frame.

Tweezers

Place every strand and crumb. "Natural" texture is meticulously arranged.

B

Lighting Micro-Adjustments

Extreme rake: drop the key almost parallel to the surface so every fibre and ridge throws a long micro-shadow. This grazing angle is the entire effect.

Barely fill: a single white card lifts the deepest shadows just enough to read — too much fill and the texture flattens to nothing.

Control

Grid or snoot the key to keep the pool tight and the falloff dramatic.

C

Composition & Camera

Angle: straight top-down flatlay so the raking light and the texture read without perspective distortion.

Focus: macro at f/16, stack 12–20 frames — at this magnification depth of field is paper-thin, so stacking is mandatory, not optional.

Frame

Compose the crop to tile or bleed — brand layouts love a seamless texture field.

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Control every reflection on the glossy surface with large diffused sources and black flags to shape the highlight edges deliberately. Tether and shoot for focus stacking so the whole reflective face stays sharp.

Prop Stylist

Source a flawless hero unit and clean the surface between every frame to kill dust and fingerprints. Stage a minimal, tonal base that supports the product without throwing unwanted colour casts onto its reflection.

Set & Assist

Rig the product dead level on a hidden mount and tape marks so we can rebuild the exact position after cleaning. Manage flags, scrims, and gloves, and keep the set airtight against dust.

Retoucher

Composite the focus stack and refine the highlight gradients so reflections read intentional and smooth. Remove residual dust and micro-scratches while preserving the true material sheen.

Styling & angle library
Arrangements
  1. Single hero centered on black acrylic for a clean mirror double
  2. Trio staggered in depth so reflections stack without touching
  3. Object on a glass shelf shot to catch a soft ceiling gradient
  4. Bottle laid on wet-look vinyl with a controlled pooled reflection
  5. Pair face-to-face, reflections meeting at the seam line
  6. Diagonal run across polished stone, reflection fading to shadow
  7. Floating on a thin acrylic riser to lift the mirror off the base
  8. Tight cluster on chrome tray, reflections read as a second cluster
Hero angles
  • Low three-quarter to maximise the reflected height
  • Dead-on eye level for a perfectly symmetrical twin
  • Slight top-down to compress the reflection into a soft base
  • Profile with a gradient sweeping the label edge
  • Raking near-tabletop angle to stretch the mirror long
Prop & set styling
  • Black acrylic sheet for the deepest, cleanest reflection
  • Frosted glass riser to break a too-perfect double
  • Dulling spray on stray hotspots that fight the label
  • Polarising the light source to tame surface glare
  • A single water droplet placed to add a crafted highlight
Finish & retouch
  • Clean the reflection of dust that the mirror doubles
  • Grade the gradient roll-off for a smooth, even fall
  • Rebuild any blown highlight edges on the label
  • Balance left/right symmetry of the reflected form
  • Fade the reflection base into pure black for a floating look
On-set checklist

The delivery package

Cut for a brand's product page and campaign — clean heroes that drop into layout, plus the texture and detail frames that sell material quality.

Three material stories

Matte form, reflective glow, and raking texture — the range that proves a photographer can handle any surface a brand throws at them.

Layout-ready

Clean sweeps and negative space shot to the brief's aspect ratios, cut-out-friendly on white.

Retouch note

Composite passes where the hero demands it — label, highlight, and edge — but keep reflections believable, not plastic.

The through-line

One discipline across all three: shape the light, flag the edges, control every reflection. Precision reads as premium.

Classic · Executive · Credible

The Executive

The board-ready headshot. Clean clamshell light and squared posture — the frame that reads competence at a glance on a leadership page.

Headshot
70mm · f/5.6
Key
45° softbox
Fill
Clamshell under
BG

A

Styling & Textures

Sharp business tailoring — navy, charcoal, or a crisp white shirt. Matte, well-pressed, simple; solids over patterns that moiré on screen.

Grooming clean and neutral, shine powdered down. The read is competence, not fashion.

Check

Collar flat, tie straight, lint rolled — the details a booker notices.

B

Lighting Micro-Adjustments

Close the clamshell: add the under-chin fill or reflector to lift eye sockets and soften lines — flattering and consistent across every sitter.

Keep it even: a low key-to-fill ratio (~2:1) for authority without harshness. Lock power and marks so frame 1 and frame 300 match.

Eyes

Position the key for a clean twin catchlight — dead eyes sink a headshot.

C

Posing Architecture & Micro-Expressions

Body: shoulders turned ~15° off-axis to slim the frame, then chin toward camera and slightly down — "forehead forward" so the sitter engages, never leans back.

Eyes: direct to lens, focus on the near iris. Talk the sitter to a genuine, settled expression.

Micro-expression

A closed, confident half-smile — warmth in the eyes, gravity in the jaw.

02
Business casual · Warm · Human

The Approachable

The team-page portrait. Softer light and an open expression — credible but human, the register modern brands actually want.

Softened, wider

A

Styling & Textures

Business casual — a soft knit, open collar, an unstructured blazer in warm neutrals. Texture and warmth over hard tailoring.

Palette lifted and friendly; nothing severe. This sitter should look like someone you'd want to email back.

Note

A touch of colour is fine here — kept muted and on-brand.

B

Lighting Micro-Adjustments

Open it up: widen and soften the key, raise the fill to ~1.5:1 for a brighter, friendlier face. Warm the background a hair.

Lift the mood: keep the whole frame a stop brighter than the Executive — light itself reads as approachability.

Feel

Aim for daylight-easy, not studio-formal.

C

Posing Architecture & Micro-Expressions

Body: relaxed shoulders, a gentle lean toward camera to signal engagement, weight easy. Let the posture breathe.

Eyes: warm and direct, with a few frames caught mid-laugh for the genuine option.

Micro-expression

A real, open smile — teeth are welcome here. Talk, don't pose, to earn it.

03
Environmental · Context · Leadership

The Environmental

The founder / leadership frame. Wider, three-quarter, with controlled context — authority set in a place, not just on grey.

Three-quarter
35–50mm
Full-length
35mm · f/4
Key

Context

A

Styling & Textures

Full look, considered head to toe — the sitter reads at three-quarter and full-length now. Tailoring that holds a confident line standing or seated.

Keep the palette controlled so any environment behind stays supporting, not competing.

Wardrobe

Watch shoes, hems, and how the jacket sits when seated — the whole figure is in frame.

B

Lighting Micro-Adjustments

Scale up: enlarge and back off the key for even coverage across a standing figure; keep the flattering direction from the headshot rig.

Control the context: light or flag the background so any environment reads soft and intentional — present, never busy. Hold separation with a rim.

Ratio

Slightly more shadow than the team-page look — a touch of gravity for leadership.

C

Posing Architecture & Micro-Expressions

Body: grounded stance — weight settled, one hand in a pocket or arms lightly crossed, shoulders open. A three-quarter turn with the face brought back to camera reads as command.

Eyes: steady to lens, assured. For seated frames, a slight forward lean keeps energy up.

Micro-expression

Composed and warm — the calm of someone used to being in charge.

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Set a warm, soft key just off-axis with a bright catchlight and light fill to keep her confident but approachable. Shoot at eye level with a slightly longer lens for flattering, trustworthy proportions.

Model

Square the shoulders slightly, lengthen the neck, and bring the chin forward and down for a strong, credible line. Give us a genuine, warm smile plus a composed neutral for range across her profiles.

MUA & Hair

Even the complexion with a natural, polished finish that holds up in close crops and video stills. Keep hair neat and framing the face so it reads professional without feeling stiff.

Stylist

Style in solid, well-fitted business colours that avoid moire and tight patterns on camera. Adjust collar, lapels, and shoulders so the tailoring sits clean when she holds the pose.

On-set checklist

The delivery package

Built for a real client day — consistent, flattering, and fast to turn around, with enough range to fill a whole leadership site from one session.

Three registers

Executive, approachable, and environmental — the same sitter tuned from board-formal to team-warm to founder-story.

Repeatable rig

Fixed marks, power, and crop so hundreds of headshots match across a company directory.

Retouch note

Clean and honest — even skin, tidy stray hairs, true colour. Executives should look like themselves on a good day.

The through-line

One flattering philosophy across all three: warm, even, credible. Consistency is the product a corporate client is buying.

Vol. 05 Fashion editorial · Magazine energy

The Movement

Attitude over stillness. The garment is the hero and it wants to move — hard light, decisive shadow, and colour used with intent for the energy an editorial page lives on.

AdvancedKit Strobe + trigger (short flash)

Baseline rig — the editorial punch

Key — Hard source

Bare-bulb, beauty dish, or a small softbox for a crisp, directional punch with defined shadow. Character over softness.

Shape — Flags + reflector

Black flags cut and carve; a single reflector opens shadow only when the story needs it.

Colour — Gels + seamless

Coloured seamless or gelled accents for graphic, campaign-grade colour blocking.

Capture

24–70mm · ISO 100 · 1/200 · f/8. Strobe to freeze fabric at its apex; burst the movement.

Starting exposureManual · 1/200–1/250 · f/8 · ISO 100 · short flash durationFreeze comes from flash duration, not shutter — drop the flash power for a shorter, sharper pop, and burst on the peak of the movement.

Motion · Fabric · Freeze

The Throw

Garment in motion. Wind, jump, or a fabric throw frozen hard by strobe at its most expressive apex.

Full length
24–35mm · f/8
Freeze
Strobe · burst
Key
Hard, high
Shape
Flags · graphic
Ground
Clean seamless
A

Styling & Textures

Choose cloth that moves and holds shape mid-air — chiffon, pleats, a structured coat with swing. Movement is the styling brief.

Bold, considered colour that reads against the seamless. This is where a statement palette earns its place.

Prep

Stylist on set for every frame — fabric resets between throws.

B

Lighting Micro-Adjustments

Go hard and high: a crisp directional key defines the fabric's folds and edges as it moves — soft light loses the drama.

Freeze it: lean on short strobe duration, not shutter, to stop the cloth clean. Flag spill to keep the ground graphic.

Timing

Burst and trigger on the rising fabric — shoot far more than you'll keep.

C

Posing Architecture & Micro-Expressions

Body: dynamic — a jump, a spin, a walk-through with intent. Strong angular limbs; the pose reads even as a silhouette.

Eyes: committed and fierce, to lens or driving the motion's direction.

Micro-expression

Editorial cool — energy in the body, control in the face.

A

Styling & Textures

Neutral or tonal wardrobe so the colour comes from light, not cloth — the gels dress the frame. Sheen and satin catch the hues beautifully here.

Skin and fabric become the canvas for two competing colours.

Test

Gel densities shift on skin — chip-test on the sitter before committing.

B

Lighting Micro-Adjustments

Split the spectrum: a warm-gelled key on one plane, a cool-gelled rim on the other, meeting on the jaw for a two-tone edge.

Protect the mix: flag the sources off each other so the colours stay pure — muddy overlap kills the effect. Gel the background for a third tone.

Balance

Keep one gel dominant; a 50/50 split reads as a mistake.

C

Posing Architecture & Micro-Expressions

Body: graphic and still — the colour is doing the work, so let the pose be a strong, clean shape that both lights carve.

Eyes: direct and cool, turned so each side of the face takes a different gel.

Micro-expression

Detached, high-fashion stillness.

03
Hard shadow · Graphic · Statement

The Statement

One hard source, deep shadow, a single graphic pose. The frame that anchors a story spread.

Three-quarter
50mm · f/9
Key
Single, bare
Fill
None
Shadow

A

Styling & Textures

Sculptural, architectural pieces — strong shoulders, sharp tailoring, a statement silhouette that hard shadow flatters.

Tonal palette so form and shadow, not colour, carry the frame.

Fit

Structure over drape — the garment must hold a line under raking hard light.

B

Lighting Micro-Adjustments

Commit to one source: a single bare or dished key, no fill, so shadow falls hard and graphic across face and cloth.

Place the shadow deliberately — its shape is a compositional element. Use a gobo or flag to shape a cast if the story wants one.

Ratio

Extreme contrast, blacks intact. Meter the highlight and let the rest go.

C

Posing Architecture & Micro-Expressions

Body: one strong, angular, held pose — a hard line the light can rake. Negative space and limb geometry do the talking.

Eyes: intense to lens, or a sharp profile that the hard edge slices.

Micro-expression

Severe, composed, unblinking.

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Freeze motion with short flash duration and shoot bursts to catch the peak of each gesture and fabric throw. Give her room in frame to move and compose for dynamic diagonals rather than static centering.

Model

Work in continuous motion, walking, turning, and throwing the garment so it flows, and exaggerate each movement past what feels natural. Reset to a strong start mark between takes so we can repeat the best shape.

MUA & Hair

Build a look and hairstyle that reads editorial in motion and survives repeated movement, with anchor points that will not collapse. Keep touch-up fast between bursts so nothing goes flat mid-sequence.

Stylist

Select pieces with movement and drape that photograph well mid-air, and rig hidden weights or tacks to control the flare. Steam and reset the garment between every take so each throw looks intentional.

Pose & direction library
Poses & body
  1. Full spin with the skirt or coat trailing wide
  2. Mid-stride walk-off toward the lens, arms swinging free
  3. Hair flip timed to the flash, head snapping back
  4. Fabric thrown up and caught at its peak float
  5. Jump with legs tucked, arms lifting for lift
  6. Sharp hip pivot leaving the shoulders behind
  7. Twirl freezing the garment in a flared bell
  8. Lunge forward with the back leg dragging cloth
  9. Arms flung wide overhead, torso arched open
  10. Running step held at the airborne apex
Expression & mimic
  • Open-mouthed exhilaration caught mid-laugh
  • Eyes closed, chin up, lost in the motion
  • Fierce direct stare through flying hair
  • Lips parted with a breath of exertion
  • Cool detachment even at full movement
  • Wind-blown squint softened into a half-smile
Directing cues
  • “Spin on three and let the fabric do whatever it wants.”
  • “Walk at me like you own the runway — don’t stop.”
  • “Big flip, then find my lens the second you land.”
  • “Throw the scarf up and forget it — I’ll catch the peak.”
  • “Keep moving, don’t settle — I want the in-between.”
  • “Jump light, chin up, breathe out at the top.”
MUA & hair
  • Long-wear base that won’t break with sweat and motion
  • Editorial graphic liner that reads even in blur
  • Loose textured hair prepped to catch air and light
  • Bold statement lip locked with setting powder
  • Strategic hairspray at the roots so movement still flows
On-set checklist

The story package

Cut as a magazine or campaign spread — energy, colour, and a graphic anchor that hold a multi-page fashion story together.

Three registers

Motion, colour, and hard statement — the beats an editorial spread paces between.

Movement library

Frozen fabric frames shot deep so the edit has the exact apex to choose.

Retouch note

Keep the drama — protect hard shadow and gel purity; over-smoothing kills editorial edge.

The through-line

Attitude and intent. Every frame reads as a point of view, not a product shot.

Whatever product is the hero — lip, lash, lid — gets the sharpest plane.

The Detail

A

Styling & Textures

The product on skin, immaculate: a clean lip line, glossed lid, defined lash. Every texture is scrutinised at this magnification.

Application reset between frames — macro forgives nothing.

Detail

Groom brows and lashes strand by strand.

B

Lighting Micro-Adjustments

Soft and close: bring a small soft source in tight for a gentle wrap and a controlled specular that shows product finish — matte, gloss, shimmer.

Ring or card fill for even, shadowless macro detail.

Specular

Place the highlight to describe the finish — it sells the texture.

C

Composition & Camera

Frame: crop tight to the hero feature — half a face, a pair of lips, one eye. Composition is graphic.

Focus: stack 4–8 frames at f/11 for a crisp plane across the curved surface.

Note

Micro-movement ruins a stack — steady the sitter and shoot fast.

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Use large, wrapping soft light and a subtle fill to render skin luminous and pore-true for a clean beauty close-up. Nail focus on the eyes and lashes and keep the background a smooth, uncluttered tone.

Model

Give micro-adjustments of the head and eyes rather than big moves, holding each position for a beat so we can lock the catchlight. Keep the face relaxed and let the skin and expression carry the frame.

MUA & Hair

This is your hero frame, so build flawless, even skin and a precise eye and lip that reward extreme close inspection. Stay on set for constant touch-ups and reset the look between every setup.

Stylist

Keep wardrobe minimal and out of the beauty crop, choosing a clean neckline that supports the face. Coordinate any visible jewellery so it complements rather than competes with the makeup.

Pose & direction library
Poses & body
  1. Tight head-and-shoulders, face square and symmetrical to lens
  2. Hands framing the jaw, fingers soft against the cheek
  3. Chin lifted slightly to lengthen the neck and open the eyes
  4. Fingertips grazing the collarbone, shoulders relaxed down
  5. Head tilted a few degrees for a gentle asymmetry
  6. One hand sweeping hair back off the face and holding
  7. Slight profile turn to feature the cheekbone and lash line
  8. Palms cradling the face from below, elbows lifted lightly
  9. Looking over the shoulder with the face returning to camera
  10. Eyes closed, face tipped toward the soft key
Expression & mimic
  • Serene neutral with the lips softly closed
  • Slow lid-drop then a clean open to the lens
  • Barely-there smile that keeps the skin calm
  • Direct, dewy gaze straight down the barrel
  • Relaxed breath with the jaw fully released
  • Eyes soft, brow smooth, no tension anywhere
Directing cues
  • “Soften your whole face — especially the space between your brows.”
  • “Close your eyes, breathe, and open on my count.”
  • “Barely lift the corners of your mouth — feel it, don’t show it.”
  • “Bring your fingers to your cheek, light as air.”
  • “Tilt your head toward the light, chin a touch up.”
  • “Let your lips part just slightly — perfect, stay.”
MUA & hair
  • Skin-first prep with glass-finish hydration under makeup
  • Sheer buildable base that lets real texture show
  • Cream products for dimensional, luminous cheeks
  • Groomed fluffy brows and clean, separated lashes
  • Hair pulled back clean so the face stays the hero
On-set checklist

The campaign package

Built for cosmetics — a glowing hero, a sculpted colour frame, and macro detail that survives packaging and billboard crops.

Three registers

Glow, sculpt, and macro — skincare through colour cosmetics from one sitting.

Crop-proof

Flawless skin and tack-sharp product detail that hold at any enlargement.

Retouch note

Clean but real — keep pores and true texture; beauty retouching is subtraction, not plastic.

The through-line

Soft, even, precise. Consistency of skin and light across the campaign.

Styling & Textures

Isolate the sell: a button, a zip, a weave, a stitch. Texture is the whole message at this crop.

Dress the section so the fabric sits and catches light naturally.

Focus

Clean the hardware — fingerprints and threads show.

B

Lighting Micro-Adjustments

Add a little rake: tilt one source off flat so weave and trim gain just enough shadow to read as texture, not print.

Card the shadow so it lifts without flattening. Enough dimension to feel the cloth.

Keep colour matched to the full-length — same garment, same truth.

Composition & Camera

Frame: crop to the hero detail on the body — pocket, cuff, collar, hem — with clean context around it.

Focus: tack-sharp on the trim or weave; a soft fall-off behind adds depth.

Note

Shoot the set the layout needs — details map to product-page callouts.

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Keep lighting consistent and repeatable so every garment matches across the catalogue, and lock exposure and white balance for the full run. Shoot standardized front, three-quarter, and detail angles on tight marks.

Model

Hit clean, consistent e-commerce poses that show fit, drape, and key features clearly. Move efficiently through the rack, resetting to the same stance so shots stay uniform across styles.

MUA & Hair

Keep hair and makeup neutral and stable so the product stays the hero across a long shoot day. Refresh lightly between changes so continuity holds from first look to last.

Stylist

Steam, pin, and clip each garment for a perfect on-model fit, hiding clips at the back for a clean front. Queue the rack in shot order and check every label, hem, and seam before she steps on the mark.

Pose & direction library
Poses & body
  1. Front-on stance showing the full garment flat and clear
  2. Three-quarter turn to reveal the side seam and fit
  3. Hand on hip to open the silhouette and show the waist
  4. Back view with a glance over the shoulder for the rear detail
  5. Walking step to show drape and movement of the fabric
  6. Tugging the hem or cuff to demonstrate length and fit
  7. Both hands in pockets to display the pocket function
  8. Arm lifted to show sleeve range and armhole cut
  9. Seated to reveal how the garment sits and folds
  10. Weight shift front to back to show the fit from two hips
Expression & mimic
  • Friendly approachable smile that keeps eyes relaxed
  • Easy neutral, lips together, catalogue-clean
  • Light laugh to add lifestyle warmth
  • Confident closed-mouth look at the lens
  • Soft glance down at the product being worn
  • Fresh, energetic open gaze between resets
Directing cues
  • “Stand tall and let the clothes hang clean — no slouch.”
  • “Turn to your side so we catch the fit, then look back at me.”
  • “Give the hem a little tug so we see the length.”
  • “Take one step and freeze — I want the drape moving.”
  • “Hand on your hip, open up the waistline for me.”
  • “Reset, breathe, and give me that easy smile again.”
MUA & hair
  • Clean natural base that reads true across many frames
  • Neutral eye and lip that never competes with product
  • Consistent, retouch-friendly finish for volume shooting
  • Simple lasting hairstyle that holds through many changes
  • Matte T-zone so shine stays even between garments
On-set checklist

The store package

A complete product listing from one pass — front, angles, and detail — consistent enough to fill a store grid without a jarring frame.

Full listing

Front, three-quarter, back, and detail per SKU — everything a product page needs.

Match-grade

Locked light, WB, and crop so the whole grid reads as one clean system.

Colour-accurate and clean; correct fit and stray threads, never fake the fabric.

The through-line

Repeatable and honest. The garment, not the mood, is the entire point.

Build the set to catch the action — the vessel, the stream, the target dish all placed for a clean pour path.

Rehearse the pour dry; mark the vessel's start position.

The Flatlay

The top-down spread. Multiple dishes composed as a graphic table — the social and editorial hero.

A

Set & Surface

Compose the whole table as a graphic arrangement — dishes, hands, linens, and props balanced for the top-down frame. Colour and negative space are the design.

Textured surface reads as the backdrop; every element placed to the grid.

Layout

Build to the crop — square for social, wide for editorial.

B

Lighting Micro-Adjustments

Soft directional from one side: a large source across the table gives even, natural light with gentle shadow that gives the spread dimension.

Fill opposite with white to keep every dish legible; keep it soft so the flatlay doesn't go flat or harsh.

Even

Watch for falloff across a big table — feather the source to cover corner to corner.

C

Angle: straight top-down on a sturdy rig or overhead arm; keep the sensor parallel to the table.

Leave a clean corner for copy or a logo.

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Light the dish with a single directional soft source and subtle backlight to bring out texture, steam, and gloss. Lock a hero camera position and shoot tethered so we can rebuild the exact frame as the food is refreshed.

Food Stylist

Build the hero plate for camera, controlling gloss, garnish, and steam, and keep backups ready to swap as it wilts. Dress the final bites with tweezers just before the frame so the food peaks on cue.

Set & Assist

Dress the tabletop with tonal surfaces and props that frame the dish without crowding it, and manage flags and reflectors. Keep the hot set clean and hand off fresh plates fast so nothing sits under the lights.

Retoucher

Composite the best textures across frames and enhance steam, gloss, and colour without making the food look artificial. Clean stray crumbs and drips while keeping the dish appetizing and true.

Styling & angle library
Arrangements
  1. Hero dish centered with negative space and a single garnish accent
  2. Full table scene with hands, cutlery and a poured drink in frame
  3. Deconstructed ingredients laid around the finished plate
  4. Stacked height build to show layers and cross-section
  5. Diagonal flow of plates leading the eye off-frame
  6. Family-style spread shot to feel abundant but curated
  7. Single spoonful lifted mid-air to show texture and steam
  8. Tight overhead grid of small plates for a menu banner
Hero angles
  • Flat-lay overhead for flat foods and full spreads
  • Forty-five degree to read both surface and height
  • Straight-on to feature stacked layers and drips
  • Low hero to make a burger or cake feel monumental
  • Raking side light angle to reveal glaze and steam
Prop & set styling
  • Matte ceramic in muted tones to keep food the hero
  • Rustic linen with intentional, natural creasing
  • Fresh herbs and crumbs scattered for lived-in realism
  • Backlight plus a mist of water for glisten and steam
  • A worn wood or stone surface for warmth and texture
Finish & retouch
  • Boost glisten on sauces and glazes selectively
  • Clean stray crumbs and drips that read as messy
  • Warm the grade slightly to keep food appetising
  • Enhance steam or add a subtle rising wisp
  • Even the plate rim and remove fingerprints
On-set checklist

The menu package

A full food story — a backlit hero, a motion frame, and a top-down spread — appetite-forward and layout-ready for menu, campaign, and social.

Three registers

Hero, action, and flatlay — the beats a food brand needs across every surface.

Layout-ready

Shot to the briefs' aspect ratios with clean space for copy.

Retouch note

Keep it appetising and honest — enhance gloss and freshness, don't fake the food.

The through-line

Backlight and meticulous styling. Freshness you can almost taste.

Vol. 09Technique · Minimal rig

The Single Source

One light, fully understood. Before you add a second head, learn what feathering, distance, and a single bounce can do — most great portraits are one light placed with intent.

BeginnerKit 1–2 lights + a modifier
TechniqueMinimal rigFeatherWrapShort vs BroadFake the second light

RelatedThe Clamshell · Rembrandt, Loop & Split · The Butterfly

Baseline — one head, one modifier

Key — One softbox

A single soft source is the whole rig. Size and distance set softness; angle sets the pattern.

Modifier discipline

Closer is softer and falls off faster; further is harder and more even. That trade is the lesson.

One passive tool

A white or black card — add or subtract — is all the "second light" a single-source frame needs.

Capture

50–85mm-equiv · ISO 100 · meter the lit cheek and let shadow fall.

Starting exposureManual · 1/160 sync · f/8 · ISO 100 · WB 5200KShutter controls ambient only — flash power sets the exposure. Sync tops out near 1/200; switch to HSS for 1/250 and up.
01
Feather · Wrap

The Feather

Rotate the source so its soft edge, not its hot core, lands on the face — the softest light a single head gives.

Crop
70mm · f/4
Key
45°, feathered
Falloff
Gentle
Tool
None
Ratio
High, natural
A

Setup & Gear

Softbox at 45° and slightly above, close enough to wrap. Aim it past the subject so only the feathered edge reaches the face.

B

The Adjustment

Rotate the box a few degrees at a time and watch the shadow side open and close. The sweet spot is even, soft, still dimensional.

C

Read & Faults

Too frontal and it flattens; too raked and the far side dies. Keep a catchlight and a whisper of nose shadow.

02
Short vs Broad

Short Light

Light the far side of the face (short) to slim and add drama; light the near side (broad) to widen. Position is the whole choice.

Crop
70mm · f/4
Key
Short side
Turn
Face off-axis
Effect
Slimming
Ratio
Moderate
A

Setup & Gear

Same single box; turn the subject, not the light. Face angled slightly away so the key falls on the far cheek.

B

The Adjustment

Short light throws the near cheek into shadow — slimming and sculptural. Rotate them back toward the light for broad, open, wider.

C

Read & Faults

Match to the face: short light flatters most; broad can help a very narrow face. Watch the nose shadow doesn't cross the lip.

03
Fake the second light

The Bounce

A white card opposite the key returns light into the shadow — one head behaving like two, with total ratio control.

Crop
70mm · f/4
Key
45°
Fill
White card
Ratio
Dial by distance
Cost
One card
A

Setup & Gear

Key at 45°; a white foamcore on the shadow side, angled to catch spill and throw it back.

B

The Adjustment

Move the card in and out to set the ratio precisely — closer lifts the shadow, further deepens it. Swap for black to subtract instead.

C

Read & Faults

The bounce should be felt, not seen. If it makes its own catchlight or flattens the form, back it off.

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Demonstrate a single source cleanly by working one light and a reflector only, and move it to show how angle and distance reshape the face. Meter carefully and keep the falloff visible as the teaching point.

Model

Hold each head position steady while the light is repositioned so the single-source effect stays readable frame to frame. Give small, patient adjustments rather than dramatic changes so the technique reads.

MUA & Hair

Keep skin matte and even so the single source shows true modelling without distracting shine. Style hair off the face so the light and shadow on the features stay clear.

Stylist

Choose simple, mid-tone wardrobe that will not bounce stray light back into the shadow side. Keep the neckline clean so the lighting on the face is the whole story.

Pose & direction library
Poses & body
  1. Face turned so the single source falls short across the far cheek
  2. Full front to the source for flat, even, shadowless light
  3. Ninety-degree profile to split the face light and dark
  4. Chin up into the source to open the eye sockets
  5. Slow rotation away to watch the shadow creep across the nose
  6. Shoulder dipped toward the source, head held level
  7. Broad-side turn with the near cheek fully lit and wide
  8. Short-side turn hiding the far cheek in falloff
  9. Head tipped back so the source rims the jaw
  10. Static neutral pose to isolate the light change only
Expression & mimic
  • Neutral hold so the study stays about the light
  • Eyes tracking the source as the face turns
  • Calm gaze straight to lens for the reference frame
  • Subtle jaw release between each rotation
  • Steady breath, no expression drift
  • Slow blink to reset the eyes between angles
Directing cues
  • “Turn a few degrees at a time — we’re chasing the shadow.”
  • “Lift your chin into the light so your eyes fill up.”
  • “Hold dead still — I’m only moving the light this time.”
  • “Face the source, flat and open — now we compare.”
  • “Give me a clean profile so it splits right down the middle.”
  • “Keep your face neutral so the light tells the story.”
MUA & hair
  • Even matte base so falloff reads without shine artefacts
  • Neutral contour that won’t confuse the natural shadow
  • Hair off the face to keep the light line clean
  • Minimal eye product so catchlights stay obvious
  • Skin-true tone so exposure comparisons hold across frames
On-set checklist

The lesson

One source, three outcomes — soft wrap, sculpted turn, controlled ratio. Master this before reaching for a second head.

Portability

This rig travels anywhere and never fights itself.

Control

Softness by distance, pattern by angle, ratio by one card.

Discipline

Fewer lights, more intent — the fastest way to improve.

Foundation

Every later volume is this, multiplied.

Vol. 10Technique · Beauty rig

The Clamshell

Two soft sources, stacked. The beauty-standard rig, drilled through the one variable that changes everything: the fill ratio between top light and bottom.

BeginnerKit 1–2 lights + a modifier
TechniqueBeauty rigTightLow ratioOpenedSculpt

RelatedClean Beauty · The Line · Activewear — In Motion

Baseline — top key, bottom fill

Key — Dish / box above

Elevated and frontal, feathered down onto the face.

Fill — Source / reflector below

Directly under the chin, facing up, filling the shadow the top light casts.

The gap

Subject sits in the "mouth" of the clamshell; the gap between the two sets the wrap.

Capture

70mm · ISO 100 · f/8 · true WB · twin catchlights.

Starting exposureManual · 1/160 sync · f/8 · ISO 100 · WB 5200KShutter controls ambient only — flash power sets the exposure. Sync tops out near 1/200; switch to HSS for 1/250 and up.
01
Tight · Low ratio

Bright & Even

Both sources close, near-equal power — the glowing, near-shadowless beauty standard.

Crop
70mm · f/8
Ratio
~1.5:1
Gap
Tight
Look
Glow
Catch
Twin
A

Setup & Gear

Dish above, reflector or second box below, both close and near-parallel to the face.

B

The Adjustment

Bring the bottom fill up until the under-shadows nearly vanish — bright, clean, low contrast.

C

Read & Faults

Twin catchlights confirm the rig. Too much bottom fill reads unnatural — keep the top dominant.

02
Opened · Sculpt

The Ratio Drop

Pull the bottom source down or off to let shadow return — the same rig, now sculptural.

Crop
70mm · f/9
Ratio
~3:1
Gap
Wider
Look
Dimensional
Catch
Top-weighted
A

Setup & Gear

Same stack; drop the bottom fill's power or distance.

B

The Adjustment

As the fill retreats, cheekbones and jaw gain shadow. Stop where structure reads but skin stays clean.

C

Read & Faults

This is the cosmetics-and-contour ratio. Too far and it stops being clamshell and becomes a hard top light.

03
Passive fill

Reflector-Only

Replace the bottom light with a reflector — cheaper, softer, and often better for natural skin.

Crop
70mm · f/8
Fill
Silver / white card
Ratio
By angle
Look
Natural glow
Cost
One card
A

Setup & Gear

Top key only; a silver or white reflector held below, angled up into the shadow.

B

The Adjustment

Tilt the card to set fill — silver for punch, white for gentle. It can never overpower the key, which keeps skin honest.

C

Read & Faults

A subject or assistant can hold it low. Watch its edge doesn't clip into frame.

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Set the clamshell with a soft source above and a fill or reflector below, balancing the ratio for glowing, even beauty light. Position the double catchlights precisely and keep her chin in the sweet spot between the two sources.

Model

Keep the head level and centered between the two sources so both catchlights sit clean in the eyes. Offer subtle chin-forward adjustments and hold still so the wrap stays even.

MUA & Hair

Prep flawless, luminous skin since the clamshell reveals every detail, and control shine that the top light will amplify. Keep hair framing softly so it does not shadow the lower fill.

Stylist

Keep wardrobe clean and simple so the beauty lighting stays the focus. Use a light neckline that supports the lower fill rather than absorbing it.

Pose & direction library
Poses & body
  1. Front-on to the clamshell for symmetrical wrap-around light
  2. Chin level, face centered between the top and bottom source
  3. Hands cradling the jaw to feature the even glow on skin
  4. Slight tilt to test how the twin catchlights shift
  5. Shoulders dropped and square for a beauty-clean base
  6. Head lifted a touch to stack both catchlights in the eyes
  7. Fingertips to collarbone, face held straight to the gap
  8. Micro three-quarter turn to keep one soft shadow edge
  9. Face tipped down to test the lower fill’s lift
  10. Static hero pose to study the wrap on the neck and jaw
Expression & mimic
  • Calm beauty neutral, lips softly closed
  • Eyes wide and open to catch the double catchlight
  • Slow lid-drop then clean re-open to lens
  • Barely-there smile keeping the face smooth
  • Relaxed brow with a settled, even gaze
  • Gentle breath so the jaw and cheeks stay soft
Directing cues
  • “Look right between the two lights — feel them wrap you.”
  • “Lift your chin till you see both sparkles in your eyes.”
  • “Keep your face square — this light loves symmetry.”
  • “Soften everything, let the glow do the work.”
  • “Tiny tilt — watch how the shadow disappears.”
  • “Open your eyes wide on my count — there they are.”
MUA & hair
  • Luminous base that plays into the wrap-around softness
  • Cream highlight on high points to amplify the glow
  • Immaculate skin prep — clamshell shows every flaw
  • Defined lashes to hold the twin catchlights
  • Hair pulled fully clear for an unbroken beauty frame

The lesson

One rig, one variable. Learn the clamshell by its ratio and you own beauty light in every register.

Standard

The most-used beauty rig, demystified.

Range

Glow to sculpt from one setup.

Cheap fill

Vol. 11Technique · Portrait patterns

Rembrandt, Loop & Split

The three shadow patterns every portrait lives in — and the exact key position that makes each. Name the pattern, place the light, own the face.

IntermediateKit 1–2 lights + a modifier
TechniquePortrait patternsSmall shadowCheek triangleHalf and half

RelatedThe Clamshell · The Butterfly · The Single Source

Baseline — one key, moved in an arc

Key — Softbox

A single soft key you walk around the subject to build each pattern.

The arc

From near-camera to 90° side, the nose shadow grows: loop → Rembrandt → split.

Height

Raise the key until the nose shadow angles down toward the mouth corner.

Capture

85mm-equiv · f/5.6 · meter the lit side.

Starting exposureManual · 1/160 sync · f/8 · ISO 100 · WB 5200KShutter controls ambient only — flash power sets the exposure. Sync tops out near 1/200; switch to HSS for 1/250 and up.
01
Small shadow

Loop

A small nose shadow that loops down toward the cheek — the most versatile, natural pattern.

Key
~30–40° side
Height
Just above eyeline
Shadow
Short loop
Use
Universal
Crop
70mm
A

Setup & Gear

Key 30–40° off camera axis, slightly above the eyes.

B

The Adjustment

Raise until the nose shadow forms a small loop pointing at the mouth corner — never touching it.

C

Read & Faults

If the loop joins the cheek shadow, you've drifted to Rembrandt. Flattering on almost everyone.

02
Cheek triangle

Rembrandt

A lit triangle on the shadow-side cheek — dramatic, classic, painterly.

Key
~45° side
Height
Higher
Mark
Cheek triangle
Use
Dramatic
Crop
70mm
A

Setup & Gear

Key to ~45° and higher, so the nose and cheek shadows meet, trapping a triangle of light under the eye.

B

The Adjustment

The triangle should be no wider than the eye and no longer than the nose. Height controls its shape.

C

Read & Faults

Needs a catchlight in the shadow-side eye or it goes dead. Slimming and moody.

03
Half and half

Split

The key at 90° — one half of the face lit, one half in shadow. Maximum drama.

Key
90° side
Height
Eyeline
Effect
Half-lit
Use
Bold, editorial
Crop
70mm
A

Setup & Gear

Key dead side-on, level with the eyes, so the shadow falls exactly down the centre line.

B

The Adjustment

A touch of negative fill on the dark side deepens the split; a whisper of bounce keeps an eye alive in the shadow.

C

Read & Faults

Keep a catchlight in the shadow eye. Powerful but severe — use with intent.

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Walk the key from short to broad to demonstrate Rembrandt, loop, and split in sequence, marking the cheek triangle each time. Keep fill and background constant so only the key angle changes as the teaching variable.

Model

Rotate the face in small, controlled increments and hold each angle so we can capture the distinct shadow pattern. Keep the same neutral expression so the lighting differences read cleanly.

MUA & Hair

Matte and even the skin so each shadow shape stays crisp and defined for the demonstration. Keep hair back so it never confuses the loop or split shadow lines.

Stylist

Dress in plain, neutral tone that keeps attention on the shifting light patterns. Avoid texture or sheen that would bounce fill into the shadow side.

Pose & direction library
Poses & body
  1. Short-side turn to drop the Rembrandt triangle on the far cheek
  2. Chin level, head angled forty-five off the key for loop shadow
  3. Full profile against the light for a clean split face
  4. Broad turn to widen the lit side and soften the loop
  5. Head rotated until the nose shadow just kisses the lip line
  6. Slight chin lift to lengthen and control the nose shadow loop
  7. Face turned so light and dark meet exactly at centre for split
  8. Shoulder angled away, head returning for the classic triangle
  9. Small tilt to test the loop drifting toward Rembrandt
  10. Static three-quarter to hold a textbook cheek triangle
Expression & mimic
  • Contemplative neutral, painterly and still
  • Eyes to the lit side to fill the shadowed eye with catchlight
  • Steady, serious gaze for the classical mood
  • Jaw relaxed to keep the shadow edges clean
  • Slow blink then hold for the reference frame
  • Soft breath, no drift, so the triangle stays put
Directing cues
  • “Turn slowly — stop when a little triangle lands on your cheek.”
  • “Keep your chin level so the nose shadow behaves.”
  • “Give me a clean profile — we’re splitting the face now.”
  • “Eyes toward the light so the dark side still sparkles.”
  • “Tiny turn back — that’s the loop becoming Rembrandt.”
  • “Hold that painterly stillness for me.”
MUA & hair
  • Matte base so shadow shapes read cleanly on the cheek
  • Subtle contour that complements the natural triangle
  • Skin-true tone for accurate light-pattern study
  • Hair kept off the cheek so the shadow shape stays visible
  • Neutral eye so the shadowed-side catchlight still pops

The lesson

Three names, one arc. Once you can call the pattern, you can build any portrait light in seconds.

Vocabulary

Name it and you can direct it.

Speed

Predict the shadow before you shoot.

Range

Natural to severe on one head.

Eyes

Always keep a shadow-side catchlight.

Glamour Falloff

Push the key higher and drop any fill for cheekbone drama and a shadowed, sultry eye.

Key
Higher
Fill
None

A

Setup & Gear

Raise the on-axis key and remove the fill.

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Place the key straight above and in front for a classic butterfly, dropping a symmetrical shadow under the nose. Add a lower reflector to control depth and keep the glamour highlights soft and even.

Model

Keep the face square to camera and the chin slightly lifted so the butterfly shadow sits centered under the nose. Give elegant, poised expressions and hold the symmetry the setup depends on.

MUA & Hair

Build a polished glamour look with sculpted cheekbones and a defined lip that the top light will flatter. Keep skin luminous but controlled so the overhead source does not blow out the forehead.

Stylist

Choose elegant, refined wardrobe with a flattering neckline that suits the glamour mood. Keep detail simple so the sculpted face stays the centerpiece.

Pose & direction library
Poses & body
  1. Face square to the overhead beauty light for symmetric butterfly shadow
  2. Chin lifted to cast the small shadow neatly under the nose
  3. Hands framing the face, elbows lifted, glamour-forward
  4. Head tipped back slightly to sculpt the cheekbones
  5. Shoulders bare and angled, face returning straight to lens
  6. Fingertips at the temple sweeping hair back and up
  7. Chin resting on the back of the hand, eyes up to camera
  8. Slow head tilt keeping the butterfly shadow centred
  9. Both hands cradling the jaw from below, chin forward
  10. Classic hero glamour pose, face lifted into the key
Expression & mimic
  • Sultry half-lidded gaze with lips softly parted
  • Confident glamour stare straight down the lens
  • Slow blink then a smoldering re-open
  • Chin-up poise with a whisper of a smile
  • Relaxed, elongated neck and settled shoulders
  • Breath held soft to keep the jaw sculpted
Directing cues
  • “Chin up into the light — feel it carve your cheekbones.”
  • “Keep your face square so the shadow sits right under your nose.”
  • “Long neck, shoulders down — give me old-Hollywood.”
  • “Half-close your eyes, then look right through me.”
  • “Lips just apart — breathe out slow.”
  • “Bring your hands up to your jaw, elbows high — gorgeous.”
MUA & hair
  • Sculpted contour and highlight for full glamour dimension
  • Strong cheekbone highlight to catch the top light
  • Bold defined lip with a precise clean edge
  • Full dramatic lashes to weight the eyes
  • Voluminous glossy hair styled with sweep and body

Gel Theory

CTO/CTB and colour gels on small, controllable sources.

Separation — Flags

Flags keep each colour on its own plane; overlap muddies.

A grey seamless takes colour cleanly; gel it for a third tone.

03
Mixed

Gel vs Clean

A true-colour key on the face against a boldly gelled background — subject natural, world coloured.

Key
Clean, true
BG
Saturated gel
Split
Skin vs set
Use
Editorial
Crop
50–70mm
A

Setup & Gear

Flagged clean key on the subject; a heavily gelled wash on the seamless behind.

C

Read & Faults

Shoot fixed WB or the camera will try to "correct" your colour away.

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Gel a clean key on her skin and drive coloured gels onto the background and rim for deliberate colour separation. Balance intensities so her complexion stays true while the colour theory reads in the shadows and edges.

Model

Angle toward the rim lights so the coloured edges catch the hair and shoulder cleanly. Hold confident, editorial expressions that carry the bold colour concept.

MUA & Hair

Keep the base makeup neutral so the gels do the colour work, and matte the skin to control coloured hotspots. Style hair with a clean edge so the rim colour rims a defined shape.

Stylist

Choose neutral or white wardrobe that will take the coloured light cleanly and show the gel tones. Avoid competing colours that would muddy the intended palette.

Pose & direction library
Poses & body
  1. Profile against a gelled rim to trace the edge in colour
  2. Front-on with warm key and cool coloured background separation
  3. Head turned into a magenta kicker on the far cheek
  4. Arms raised overhead to catch the coloured back edge
  5. Shoulder pressed to camera, colour rimming the jaw and neck
  6. Slow lean into a two-tone crossed-gel wash
  7. Chin down, eyes up, colour skimming the hairline
  8. Back to camera, head half-turned into the coloured beam
  9. Hands sweeping through hair lit by a cyan edge
  10. Static pose splitting warm face and cool rim
Expression & mimic
  • Cool detached editorial stare
  • Eyes cast toward the coloured source
  • Lips parted, moody and still
  • Intense direct gaze through the wash
  • Half-lidded calm holding the mood
  • Slow blink then lock to lens
Directing cues
  • “Turn your cheek into the colour — let it kiss the edge.”
  • “Keep it moody — the colour brings the drama, not the smile.”
  • “Lift your arms so the coloured light finds your outline.”
  • “Look toward the glow, then slowly back to me.”
  • “Hold still — I’m balancing warm on you and cool behind.”
  • “Chin down, eyes up — catch that rim in your gaze.”
MUA & hair
  • Neutral true base so gels read as the intended hue on skin
  • Metallic or reflective accents to bounce coloured light
  • Glossy skin finish to pick up the coloured edges
  • Graphic liner that survives under saturated wash
  • Sleek hair with a defined edge to catch the rim colour
On-set checklist

The lesson

Colour is placed, flagged, and balanced — never splashed. One dominant tone always wins.

Intent

Accent, two-tone, or mixed — all deliberate.

Separation

Flags keep colours pure.

WB

Lock it or lose the effect.

Restraint

One colour leads; the rest support.

Place a cutter or object between a hard source and the subject to cast a shaped shadow.

B

The Adjustment

Distance sets the pattern's sharpness — gobo close to subject for crisp, near the light for soft. Compose the shadow as part of the frame.

C

Read & Faults

The pattern should support, not confuse — keep the eyes clear.

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Use a small, undiffused source for crisp hard light with sharp-edged shadows and punchy contrast. Position it precisely and remove fill so the graphic shadow shapes stay the point of the image.

Model

Hold strong, deliberate angles since hard light rewards clean lines and precise positioning. Keep still through each frame so the sharp shadow edges stay exactly where we placed them.

MUA & Hair

Matte the skin thoroughly because hard light will exaggerate every shine and texture. Sculpt clean definition that reads well under the unforgiving edge of the source.

Stylist

Choose clean, structured wardrobe that casts and holds strong shadow shapes. Keep it simple so the hard light and its shadows lead the frame.

Pose & direction library
Poses & body
  1. Sharp profile to let hard light cut a crisp shadow line
  2. Hand raised so its shadow slices hard across the face
  3. Chin down with the brow casting a defined eye shadow
  4. Head turned to throw a knife-edge nose shadow
  5. Fingers splayed near the cheek for a crisp cast pattern
  6. Shoulder angled into the sun-gun for a hard rim line
  7. Face half in blade of light, half in clean dark
  8. Arms crossed, hard shadow etching the forearm edges
  9. Slight lean so the shadow of a prop rakes the jaw
  10. Static square pose to showcase raw undiffused contrast

  • Steely unsmiling intensity
  • Eyes narrowed against the hard beam
  • Jaw set, gaze direct and defiant
  • Lips pressed, no softness
  • Cool stare into the shadow side
  • Held breath for a rigid, graphic stillness
Directing cues
  • “Turn until the shadow cuts a clean line down your face.”
  • “Raise your hand slow — watch the shadow slice across you.”
  • “Give me hard — jaw set, no smile, pure edge.”
  • “Chin down so your brow throws a strong shadow.”
  • “Hold dead still — this light is unforgiving and I love it.”
  • “Stare into the dark side like you’re daring it.”
MUA & hair
  • Matte base only — hard light exaggerates every shine
  • Strong sculpted brow to read in high contrast
  • Precise graphic liner that holds its edge
  • Flawless skin prep since hard light shows all texture
  • Sleek defined hair to cast clean, deliberate shadows

The lesson

Hard light makes shadow a design element. Control its edge with source size, its shape with cutters.

Edge

Shape

Texture

Great on cloth and structure.

Compose

The shadow is part of the frame.
