On-set crew brief
Photographer

Blow the background to pure white with separately metered background lights while keeping a soft, clean key on her. Guard against flare spilling onto the subject so she stays crisp against the seamless white.

Model

Keep energy light and airy to match the high-key mood, with open, buoyant expressions. Watch your edges against the white and keep gestures clean so nothing gets lost in the brightness.

MUA & Hair

Give fresh, radiant skin and soft definition that reads against the bright field without washing out. Keep hair tidy so its edge separates cleanly from the white background.

Stylist

Avoid pure white wardrobe that would merge with the background, choosing soft tones with enough edge to separate. Keep the styling clean and light to suit the high-key feel.

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Work a single controlled source with heavy negative fill and a black background for a moody low-key result. Feather the light so only the essential planes of the face emerge from the shadow.

Model

Move slowly into the pool of light and hold introspective, quiet expressions that suit the darkness. Let small turns reveal just an edge of the face so the mood stays low and deliberate.

MUA & Hair

Keep skin matte and definition subtle so the sliver of light reads as sculpted rather than shiny. Style hair to fall into shadow so it deepens the low-key frame.

Stylist

Dress in dark, textured tones that recede into the shadow and let the lit face carry the frame. Avoid bright accents that would pull attention from the pool of light.

  • “Drop your chin, let one eye find the light.”
  • “Breathe out slow — let the mood settle into the black.”
  • “Emerge toward me a hair — there, that’s the frame.”
MUA & hair

  • Dark or muted lip that recedes into the shadow
  • Hair kept dark and close to melt into the black

The lesson

Low-key is subtraction, not underexposure. Light one thing, kill everything else, keep detail in the dark.

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Set a rim or hair light behind her to carve a bright edge and separate her from a dark ground. Flag the backlight off the lens and add just enough front fill to keep the face readable.

Model

Position so the backlight catches the profile and hairline, turning your head to find the strongest edge. Hold the angle steady so the rim stays clean and continuous.

MUA & Hair

Style hair with a defined silhouette since the backlight will rim its outline and reveal flyaways. Keep skin controlled so the small amount of fill renders it evenly.

Stylist

Choose wardrobe with an interesting edge or texture at the shoulders for the rim to catch. Keep colours dark enough to separate from the bright backlit edge.

Continuous vs Strobe

Freeze it or feel it. How light source and shutter together decide whether motion reads as tack-sharp, streaked, or cinematic — the last technical lever in the studio.

AdvancedKit Strobe + trigger (short flash)
TechniqueMotionFreezeTrailCinematic

RelatedThe Movement · Activewear — In Motion · The Power

Baseline — the motion levers

Strobe — Flash duration

Short flash duration (t.1) freezes motion regardless of shutter.

Continuous — Shutter rules

With constant light, the shutter alone decides sharp or blurred.

Mixing

Slow shutter + strobe = a sharp core with a motion trail (dragged shutter).

Capture

trigger and burst; test flash duration on your heads.

Setup & Gear

Strobes set to low power (shorter flash duration) in a darker room so ambient can't smear the frame.

It's flash duration, not shutter, that freezes — drop power for a shorter, sharper pop. Burst and trigger on the peak.

Source

Shutter
Slow

Use
Dynamic

Setup & Gear

Strobe for the sharp exposure plus enough ambient (or a continuous head) to register during a slow shutter.

03
Cinematic

Continuous

Constant light and shutter control for natural motion blur and a filmic, what-you-see feel.

Source
Continuous
Shutter
Chosen blur
Result
Natural motion
Use
Cinematic
Crop
35–85mm
A

Setup & Gear

Continuous LED or tungsten so exposure is entirely shutter-driven — and you see the light as it'll render.

B

The Adjustment

Pick the shutter for the motion you want — fast for sharp, slow for blur. What you see is what you get, the continuous advantage.

C

Read & Faults

Continuous is dimmer than strobe — expect higher ISO or wider apertures, and bridges neatly to video.

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Demonstrate the difference by shooting the same movement first under continuous light for motion blur, then under strobe to freeze it. Keep framing and exposure comparable so the blur-versus-freeze contrast is the clear takeaway.

Model

Repeat the same controlled movement consistently so the continuous and strobe frames are directly comparable. Vary speed on cue so we can show a range of blur and a crisp freeze.

MUA & Hair

Build a look and hair that hold up through repeated movement across both lighting setups. Anchor the style so it stays consistent when we switch from continuous to strobe.

Stylist

Select wardrobe with movement that shows blur beautifully under continuous light and freezes cleanly under strobe. Reset the garment between takes so each pass reads the same.

Pose & direction library
Poses & body
  1. Hair toss held mid-arc to compare freeze versus smear
  2. Fabric swished side to side for a motion-blur trail
  3. Hand waved across the face for a controlled streak
  4. Slow walk toward lens to show continuous drag
  5. Sharp head snap frozen crisp under strobe
  6. Twirl repeated for both a blur pass and a frozen pass
  7. Arm sweep overhead tracing a lit motion line
  8. Jump caught tack-sharp at the apex under flash
  9. Body sway held so ambient smears while flash freezes
  10. Static core with only the hands in deliberate motion
Expression & mimic
  • Energetic open expression for the motion frames
  • Focused calm for the frozen strobe capture
  • Eyes tracking the movement direction
  • Lips parted with the effort of the swing
  • Confident stare held through the blur
  • Quick reset to neutral between passes
Directing cues
  • “Same move twice — once slow for the blur, once sharp for the freeze.”
  • “Toss your hair on three — I’ll catch it two ways.”
  • “Keep your core still, let just your hands travel.”
  • “Walk at me steady — don’t stop for the drag shot.”
  • “Big snap and hold — the flash will nail you crisp.”
  • “Sway slow so the room streaks while you stay sharp.”
MUA & hair
  • Long-wear base that holds through repeated motion takes
  • Bold features that read even in a motion smear
  • Loose textured hair that trails cleanly on the toss
  • Setting spray to survive multiple energetic passes
  • Defined lip locked so it stays crisp on the freeze
On-set checklist

The lesson

Two independent levers — flash duration and shutter. Together they place any motion anywhere from frozen to flowing.

Freeze

Short flash duration, dark room.

Trail

Strobe core, dragged shutter.

Cinematic

Continuous, shutter-driven.

Bridge

Continuous crosses into video.

The Type

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Light clean and natural at eye level so casting directors read her real face and range clearly. Capture distinct, castable types across a few setups without stylising away her authenticity.

Model

Deliver a range of honest, castable expressions from warm to serious, each landing in the eyes. Keep movements small and grounded so every frame reads as a usable actor look.

MUA & Hair

Keep makeup natural and true to how she really looks so the headshot matches the room. Style hair simply and consistently so continuity holds across type changes.

Stylist

Choose simple, solid wardrobe in a few necklines that suggest castable types without costume. Keep it timeless and fitted so the shots stay usable for a long time.

Pose & direction library
Poses & body
  1. Clean tight framing, shoulders square, castable and honest
  2. Slight turn with the eyes returning fully to lens
  3. Relaxed natural set that lets the true face read
  4. Chin level, no tricks, an open commercial look
  5. Micro-shift to a warmer, more approachable angle
  6. Subtle lean in to close the distance to camera
  7. Straight-on serious look for the dramatic range
  8. Head tilt for the lighter, comedic type read
  9. Shoulders relaxed down for an unguarded presence
  10. Static hero frame that shows the actor as themselves
Expression & mimic
  • Warm approachable commercial smile
  • Grounded dramatic neutral with intent behind the eyes
  • Subtle range shift from serious to open on cue
  • Genuine spark of life in the eyes to lens
  • Relaxed authentic resting face, no mask
  • Slow blink then a fresh, present re-engage
Directing cues
  • “Give me your commercial look — the one that books the ad.”
  • “Now the dramatic side — something’s at stake behind your eyes.”
  • “Just be you for a second — that’s what casting wants.”
  • “Think a thought, don’t act it — let it flicker.”
  • “Small lean toward me, eyes right down the lens.”
  • “Reset, breathe, and give me alive-and-present.”
MUA & hair
  • Skin-true minimal base — casting must see the real face
  • No heavy contour that would mislead on type
  • Groomed natural brows kept honest
  • Bare or barely-tinted lip in the true tone
  • Hair in the actor’s real, castable everyday style

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Light with edge and atmosphere that matches her sound, using colour, haze, and contrast to build the musician mood. Shoot loose and reactive to catch attitude and the energy of performance.

Model

Perform to camera as you would to a crowd, letting the instrument and body language carry the attitude. Keep the energy authentic and give us moments between the big poses too.

MUA & Hair

Build a look with edge that suits her genre and survives movement and stage energy. Keep it tactile and lived-in rather than overly polished so it reads as real performance.

Stylist

Style the wardrobe to match the music and her stage identity, layering texture and signature pieces. Rig instruments and accessories so they sit and hang right in frame.

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Light to reveal the full line of the body and freeze the peak of each movement with short flash duration. Give her space and compose for the long, extended shapes a dancer creates.

Model

Extend fully through fingertips and toes and hold the peak of each shape so we can capture clean lines. Reset and repeat the movement so we can catch it at its strongest point.

MUA & Hair

Keep the look clean and secure so nothing distracts from the line or collapses mid-movement. Anchor the hair so it holds the intended shape through repeated jumps and turns.

Stylist

Choose wardrobe that reveals and follows the body line, with fabric that flows on the movement. Fit it close and secure so it never obscures the shape at the peak.

Pose & direction library
Poses & body
  1. Full extension in a leap, toes pointed, body a single line
  2. Arabesque held clean with the working leg fully stretched
  3. Mid-turn with the skirt or hair spiralling out
  4. Deep back-bend cambré framing the arched throat
  5. Pointed foot lifted, arms in a soft third position
  6. Contraction curl then release for a modern line
  7. Grand battement kick frozen at its highest point
  8. Floor pose with limbs stretched into elegant diagonals
  9. Port de bras sweep tracing a lit arc through the air
  10. Sustained balance on demi-pointe, spine impossibly long
Expression & mimic
  • Serene focus that hides the physical effort
  • Eyes following the leading hand’s line
  • Chin lifted with a proud, extended neck
  • Soft ecstatic release at the peak of movement
  • Calm inward gaze for a lyrical mood
  • Controlled breath masking the exertion
Directing cues
  • “Lengthen through your fingertips — make the line endless.”
  • “Jump on my count and hold the shape at the very top.”
  • “Point everything — toes, fingers, focus.”
  • “Let your face stay calm even though your body is working.”
  • “Turn slow so I catch the fabric drawing the line.”
  • “Breathe into the balance — grow taller as you hold.”
MUA & hair
  • Sweat-proof base built for full-body exertion
  • Clean elegant eye that reads across a wide frame
  • Sleek secured hair or bun that holds through leaps
  • Natural luminous skin to catch the line-defining light
  • Soft rosy lip that suits the dancer’s grace

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Use hard, directional light and low angles to sculpt muscle and project power and scale. Add haze and rim to heroize her form and shoot for peak physical tension.

Model

Engage the muscles and hold strong, powerful stances that show tension and physical control. Bring genuine intensity in the eyes so the strength reads as attitude, not just pose.

MUA & Hair

Prep the skin with a controlled sheen so the hard light defines muscle without looking greasy. Keep hair secure and out of the way so it holds through exertion.

Stylist

Choose athletic wardrobe that reveals and flatters the physique and moves with her. Fit it tight and tacked so it stays clean during dynamic, high-tension poses.

  1. Explosive sprint start frozen at the drive
  2. Mid-lift with muscles flexed and braced
  3. Ready crouch coiled for the first move

  5. Sport-specific action held at its peak tension
  6. Chest heaving, hands on knees in triumphant recovery
  7. Arms raised in a victory stance, sweat catching light
  8. Torso twist mid-throw with the whole body engaged

  10. Static hero pose flexing the trained physique

  • Gritted determination at maximum effort

  • Calm, dangerous pre-competition focus
  • Sweat-and-strain intensity in the eyes
  • Steely confidence with the jaw set
Directing cues
  • “Give me the face you make on the last rep.”
  • “Explode on three and freeze at the top of the drive.”
  • “Flex like it’s the moment before the whistle.”
  • “Eyes on me — that’s the game-face I want.”
  • “Big breath, brace your whole core, and hold the power.”
  • “Let me see the effort — don’t hide the strain.”
MUA & hair

  • Hair secured tight and stage-ready for motion
  • Minimal skin-true makeup to keep it authentic and strong
  • Groomed brows framing an intense, focused gaze

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Light soft and warm to celebrate the silhouette of the bump, using backlight and gentle wrap for a glowing profile. Direct with care and patience, offering rest between setups and keeping her comfortable throughout.

Model

Frame the bump with your hands and turn to profile so the form reads as the centerpiece. Take breaks whenever you need and let the expressions stay tender and unhurried.

MUA & Hair

Give a soft, glowing, natural finish that celebrates her radiance rather than masking it. Keep touch-ups gentle and quick so she can rest comfortably between frames.

Stylist

Choose flowing, form-revealing pieces that flatter and frame the bump beautifully. Have comfortable options ready and adjust the drape so she feels at ease and celebrated.

Pose & direction library
Poses & body
  1. Both hands cradling the belly from the sides, weight settled
  2. Profile turn to feature the silhouette of the bump
  3. One hand under and one above the belly, framing gently
  4. Seated with the belly resting soft into the lap
  5. Standing three-quarter, hands forming a heart on the bump
  6. Backlit profile with a flowing gown tracing the curve
  7. Leaning back slightly to lengthen and lift the belly line
  8. Partner’s hands joining hers around the bump if present
  9. Gaze down toward the belly, hands wrapped protectively
  10. Chin lifted, hands low, a serene glowing full-length pose

  • Soft glowing serenity, eyes calm
  • Tender gaze down toward the belly
  • Quiet joyful smile, private and warm
  • Eyes closed, face lifted, peaceful
  • Gentle direct gaze full of anticipation
  • Slow breath with the shoulders relaxed and open
Directing cues
  • “Cradle the bump the way you do when no one’s watching.”
  • “Turn to your side so we see that beautiful silhouette.”
  • “Look down at your baby and just feel it for a second.”
  • “Breathe slow — let that glow settle in.”
  • “Lengthen your spine and lift the bump toward the light.”
  • “Soft smile — think of meeting them.”

  • Soft romantic waves with easy movement and shine

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Work slowly with soft, flattering light and keep continuous check-ins, showing her frames often so she stays in control of the shoot. Protect privacy on a closed set and only ever direct toward what she has said she is comfortable with.

Model

Posing here is fully collaborative, so we build every pose together and you can pause, adjust, or stop at any moment. Move at your own pace and lean into whatever makes you feel celebrated and at ease.

MUA & Hair

Create a soft, natural look that makes her feel like the best version of herself, checking comfort as you work. Keep touch-ups calm and respectful of her space so the mood stays safe and unhurried.

Stylist

Offer tasteful options she has pre-approved and let her choose what feels right, never pushing beyond her stated comfort. Provide a robe and privacy for every change so she feels safe and respected throughout.

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Shoot the blue hour and early golden light when the city glass turns warm, and bounce a silver reflector to lift shadow from harsh overhead sun between buildings. Watch for background clutter and passing traffic, and use long lenses to compress the streetscape behind her.

Model

Bring layered pieces that read against concrete and glass and shoes you can genuinely walk in on uneven pavement. Angle your face slightly away from direct sun to soften squinting, and let arms and hips break the vertical lines of the architecture.

MUA & Hair

Set the base with a long-wear matte foundation and blotting layer so midday heat and city grime do not break the finish. Keep hair in a sculpted style with flexible hold that survives wind funnelling between towers.

Stylist

Choose a palette that lifts off grey urban tones, favouring saturated coats or crisp tailoring over busy prints. Pack lint rollers, tape and pins because street shooting shows every wrinkle in raking light.

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Work the first and last hours of light when the sand glows and the sky has colour, and use a large reflector or scrim to tame the hard reflected glare off water and sand. Shoot into the light for rim-lit hair and keep a lens cloth handy for salt spray.

Model

Bring wardrobe that moves in a sea breeze and secondary pieces in case wind or spray makes one look unworkable. Plant your feet in the sand for stability, let fabric catch the wind, and turn your face to keep hair off the eyes rather than fighting every gust.

MUA & Hair

Use waterproof, sweat-resistant products and a hydrating primer so the base does not slide in humidity and heat. Prep hair with anti-humidity product and carry pins and a soft tie to manage flyaways between frames.

Stylist

Select breathable, flowing fabrics and beach-appropriate layers that photograph clean against sand and water. Bring double-sided tape and weights, since even light coastal wind lifts hems and reveals fit issues.

  8. Wade knee-deep, arms out for balance, torso twisting to camera
  9. Sit on driftwood or rock, knees drawn up, chin resting on them

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Chase the dappled shafts and soft green fill under the canopy, and carry a reflector to open the deep shade on her face where light falls unevenly. Meter carefully for the bright sky gaps and consider a low ISO tripod frame in the darker undergrowth.

Model

Wear layers suited to cooler, damp forest air and footwear that grips mossy roots and soft ground. Use trees and fallen logs as anchors for grounded, rooted poses, and tilt your face toward the brightest canopy gaps to catch the light.

MUA & Hair

Choose a dewy but long-wear base that reads warm against cool green shade, and keep a matting powder for humidity. Style hair with soft texture that suits the organic setting and pin any pieces that catch on branches.

Stylist

Lean into earthy, textural wardrobe that harmonises with bark, moss and foliage rather than fighting it. Bring a groundsheet, wipes and a spare hem so damp forest floor and burrs do not mark the pieces.

  4. Walk a soft dirt path away, glancing back over the shoulder
  5. Lean against a broad trunk, head tipped back, throat exposed to canopy light
  6. Crouch low among ferns, forearms on knees, gaze up through the leaves
  7. Wind cue: let a loose sleeve or hem drift as a gust moves the branches
  8. Sit on a low rock, knees together, hands loose, framed by green depth behind
  9. Reach one hand up to a hanging branch, body stretched into a long line
  10. Turn slowly through a shaft of light, hair catching the beam

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Build the effect in-camera with prisms, gels, fabric drags and slow-sync flash rather than leaving it all to post. Lock your exposure and focus first, then experiment with foreground refractions so she stays sharp behind the chaos.

Model

Hold strong, deliberate poses and expressions for longer, since dragged shutters and layered effects reward stillness in the subject. Trust the process when coloured light or motion blur passes across you and keep your eyeline exactly where directed.

MUA & Hair

Keep makeup graphic and clean so it survives coloured gels without muddying, and consider reflective or metallic accents that play with the light tricks. Set everything firmly because effect frames often mean repeated takes.

Stylist

Choose surfaces that interact with light, sequins, PVC, satin and sheer layers that catch refraction and colour. Keep silhouettes bold and readable so the styling survives when the frame gets busy with effects.

Pose & direction library
Poses & body
  1. Press a palm and cheek to glass for a distorted, intimate frame
  2. Pose behind a sheer or textured layer that veils and reveals the body line
  3. Hold a small mirror to fracture the face into the composition
  4. Freeze mid-gesture as a prism throws a rainbow across the skin
  5. Reach a hand toward the lens for forced-perspective scale play
  6. Silhouette against a saturated gel wash, body as pure shape
  7. Interact with a fan-blown fabric that streaks color through the frame
  8. Coil low then extend into a long diagonal for a motion-blur pull
  9. Split light and shadow on the face with a hard slatted gobo
  10. Hold perfectly still inside a projected pattern mapped across the skin
Expression & mimic
  • Neutral, sculptural face — let the light do the drama
  • One eye catching a colored beam, the other in shadow
  • Lips parted, breath held, as the effect resolves
  • Slow, deliberate blink synced to the shutter
  • Gaze following the prism color across the frame
  • Cool detachment straight to lens through the veiling layer
Directing cues
  • “Hold it right there — the color’s landing on your cheek.”
  • “Push your hand to me — big and close, don’t be shy.”
  • “Move slow through the light so it streaks.”
  • “Eyes to where the rainbow is falling.”
  • “Stay statue-still — let the pattern wrap you.”
  • “Press into the glass — a little more, cheek and all.”
MUA & hair
  • Clean matte base so colored gels read true on the skin
  • A metallic or foil lid to bounce the experimental light
  • Sleek sculpted hair so shapes stay clean in silhouette
  • Graphic liner or a wet-look accent that survives extreme lighting
  • Strobing highlight on the high planes to catch prism color

100mm macro

A

Styling & Wardrobe

Feature a scalloped lace edge, an embroidered motif or a satin strap resting across the collarbone or forearm. Lint-roll every fibre and set the strap tension so the trim sits taut against the skin without pressing a mark.

B

Lighting Micro-Adjustments

Skim a narrow strip box almost parallel to the surface so raking light reveals the thread relief and picot edge. A small silver card returns just enough fill to keep the deepest lace apertures from crushing to black.

C

Posing & Micro-Expressions

Ask for stillness and controlled breath so the fabric does not shift during the shallow-focus capture. Use a subtle limb rotation to align the trim with the plane of sharpest focus.

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Light soft and directional to sculpt form with taste and restraint, keeping the mood intimate rather than explicit. Shoot at her comfortable pace, confirm each frame is respectful, and favour elegant crops over gratuitous ones.

Model

Work with elongated, graceful lines and relaxed shoulders that flatter the cut of the pieces. Communicate your comfort limits freely, and let hands and gaze carry quiet confidence rather than force.

MUA & Hair

Keep skin luminous and even from face to décolletage and body so tone matches under soft light. Style hair in a soft, undone finish that feels intimate without covering the garment lines.

Stylist

Fit each piece precisely to her body with discreet clips and correct sizing, since intimate apparel lives or dies on fit. Have a robe on hand between setups and steam every seam so the fabric sits perfectly.

Pose & direction library
Poses & body
  1. Recline on soft bedding, one knee drawn up, weight rolled onto a hip for a long flattering line
  2. Sit on the edge of the bed, back arched gently, hands framing the waist
  3. Stand three-quarter to camera, one hand at the collarbone, shoulders soft and open
  4. Kneel with an elongated spine, chin lifted, arms tracing the silhouette
  5. Lie on the front propped on forearms, ankles crossed and lifted behind
  6. Turn away to show the back detail, glancing over the shoulder
  7. Drape in a sheer robe half-slipped off one shoulder, hands holding it loosely closed
  8. Cross the legs seated, torso twisted for an S-curve through the body
  9. Reach both arms overhead against soft light for a lengthened waist
  10. Curl into a relaxed side-lying pose, one hand cradling the head
Expression & mimic
  • Lids low and relaxed, a soft unforced half-smile
  • Slow breath that lifts the chest gently, gaze downcast then up
  • Quiet confident look straight to lens
  • Lips just parted, chin tipped toward the shoulder
  • Eyes closed one beat, face turned to the window light
  • Serene, self-possessed — no tension in the jaw
Directing cues
  • “Roll onto your hip — long through the waist, breathe out.”
  • “This is your space, your morning — nothing to prove.”
  • “Soft chin down, then lift your eyes to me slowly.”
  • “Let the robe fall where it wants — hold it easy.”
  • “Point the toe, lengthen the leg — beautiful line.”
  • “Shoulders back and down — you’re completely at ease.”
MUA & hair
  • Second-skin base with a lit-from-within finish, no heavy mask
  • Soft rosy blush and a nude satin lip for an intimate look
  • Undone, touchable hair — loose waves or a soft pillow-texture
  • Body luminizer on collarbones, shoulders and shins to define the line
  • Groomed brows and fluttery natural lashes, nothing harsh

Photographer

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Expose carefully to hold detail in the white gown without clipping the highlights, using fill to keep the fabric texture alive. Capture full-length silhouettes and detail passes of lace, train and beading in the same lighting setup.

Model

MUA & Hair

Create a flawless, photograph-proof bridal base that reads timeless rather than trend-driven, with soft luminous skin. Build a secure hairstyle that holds through movement and complements the neckline and any veil.

Stylist

Steam the gown thoroughly and manage it with white gloves to avoid marks on delicate fabric. Have clips at the back for a clean front fit, and keep the train, veil and jewellery styled and ready.

Streetwear — The Attitude

Streetwear lives on attitude, graphic energy and colour, and the light should be bold and unafraid. The direction leans into hard shadow, saturated gels and full-body motion to match the culture it serves.

IntermediateKit 1–2 lights + a modifier
FashionStreetwearGRAPHICHARDCOLOURGEL

RelatedThe Movement · Activewear — In Motion · Avant-Garde — The Concept

Baseline — Streetwear

Own the Shadow

Use hard light and shape so shadow becomes a deliberate graphic element.

Colour Bold

Push gelled colour with intent while keeping the garment fabric readable.

Real Energy

Direct movement and stance so the attitude reads lived-in and confident.

Capture

A

Styling & Wardrobe

Layer an oversized graphic hoodie, cargo and cap with strong silhouette and bold logo placement. Style the layers so the hard shadow cuts across clean shapes rather than busy clutter.

B

Rake a gridded bare head hard from the side to throw a sharp, deliberate cast shadow. A gobo or set element shapes that shadow into a graphic that plays with the wardrobe.

C

Adopt a wide, grounded stance with weight low so the silhouette reads strong. Keep a cool, direct gaze that owns the frame and the attitude.

Gel a magenta key from camera-left and a cyan rim from behind for a split colour wash. Keep a small ungelled kicker on the face so skin stays believable amid the colour.

03
ENERGY · FULL

Full Motion

A full-length action frame that captures movement and streetwear energy.

Key
Bare strobe
Ratio
4:1
Aperture
f/9

A

Styling & Wardrobe

Style loose layers and a light jacket that flare and swing during a jump or spin. Lace and secure everything so the movement reads dynamic without wardrobe failure.

B

Lighting Micro-Adjustments

Freeze motion with a short-duration bare strobe so garment flare stays sharp. Add a rim so the flying fabric separates cleanly against a brighter mid background.

C

Posing & Micro-Expressions

Shoot bursts through a jump, pivot or walk-off to catch peak silhouette and swing. Keep the expression charged and present so the energy feels real.

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Shoot with bold contrast and a low, confident angle that gives the looks presence and edge. Embrace hard light and urban texture, and direct strong stances that let the attitude of the styling lead.

Model

Own the frame with grounded, assertive posture and a direct, cool gaze that carries the streetwear mood. Play with layering gestures, tugging a hood or hem, so the oversized silhouettes read intentional.

MUA & Hair

Keep skin real and matte with a subtly defined, editorial finish that supports an attitude-driven look. Style hair with texture and edge that suits the streetwear register without going precious.

Stylist

Balance proportion in oversized layering so the silhouette stays deliberate rather than sloppy. Style hardware, sneakers and accessories as statement details and pin drape so it falls exactly as intended.

Pose & direction library
Poses & body
  1. Wide stance, arms crossed, chin dropped for a low-angle power frame
  2. Lean into a graffiti wall, one knee bent, hood up
  3. Mid-stride with an oversized jacket swinging open
  4. Sit on concrete steps, legs spread wide, elbows on knees
  5. Hand tugging a drawstring or cap brim, face half-shadowed
  6. Over-the-shoulder turn with a hard, direct stare
  7. Crouch low against a chain-link fence, fingers hooked in the mesh
  8. Layered-fit reveal — open the outer layer to show what’s under
  9. Lean on a railing, weight thrown back, one foot forward
  10. Big gestural walk toward the lens, jacket and hair in motion
Expression & mimic
  • Cold, unimpressed stare into the lens
  • Slow smirk building at one corner of the mouth
  • Jaw set, chin low, eyes up under the brow
  • Quick attitude-glance over the shoulder
  • Deadpan neutral, all in the posture
  • A flash of real grin breaking the cool
Directing cues
  • “Chin down, eyes up — give me nothing, that’s the look.”
  • “Widen the stance — take up all the space.”
  • “Walk at me hard, let the jacket move.”
  • “Tug the cap, half your face in shadow.”
  • “Slow smirk — like you know something I don’t.”
  • “Throw it over the shoulder — cold stare, hold it.”
MUA & hair
  • Matte skin with sculpted contour for a hard-edged read
  • A graphic liner flick or smudged grunge eye
  • Slicked baby hairs or a bold defined texture
  • Deep matte or glossy dark lip for attitude
  • Strong brushed-up brows to anchor the face

Vol. 36Fashion · Editorial

Avant-Garde — The Concept

Avant-garde work trades product clarity for idea, sculpture and mood, and the light becomes a co-author. The direction stays bold and conceptual while always treating the model as a collaborator, never a prop.

AdvancedKit 1–2 lights + a modifier
FashionEditorialSCULPTUREHARDCONCEPTSHADOW

RelatedBold Makeup — The Colour Story · Streetwear — The Attitude · Activewear — In Motion

Baseline — Avant-Garde

Idea First

Let the concept lead and shape light, set and pose around the single idea.

Sculpt Boldly

Use one committed source so form and shadow read as deliberate sculpture.

Collaborate

Brief the model fully so the extreme direction is understood and consensual.

Capture

RF 85mm f/1.2L · f/8 · 1/160 · ISO 100.

SCULPTURE · HARD

Styling & Wardrobe

Choose a structural garment with strong architecture and matte surface that holds shape. Sculpt hair and remove clutter so the silhouette reads as a single clean form.

Place one gridded bare head to graze the form so most of the frame falls to deep shadow. Heavy negative fill on all sides keeps the sculpture crisp and the black true.

03
BEAUTY · CROSSOVER

Beauty Cross

A beauty-fashion crossover where sculptural light meets refined skin and make-up.

Key
Clamshell
Ratio
3:1
Aperture
f/9

100mm macro
Tone

A

Styling & Wardrobe

Pair a conceptual make-up or headpiece with a sculptural collar so beauty and fashion meet. Keep skin prep flawless and edges clean so the crossover reads considered.

B

Lighting Micro-Adjustments

Set an on-axis beauty key with an under-chin fill for glowing, dimensional skin. Add a subtle rim so the headpiece and jaw edge separate from the background.

C

Square the face to the beauty key and lift the chin a touch for the flattering plane. Coach micro-shifts of the eyes and lips so the beauty read stays alive.

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Light to sculpt the sculptural garment forms, using dramatic contrast that emphasises shape over comfort. Compose with negative space and unusual crops so the concept, not convention, drives the frame.

Model

Hold strong, sometimes uncomfortable architectural poses that echo the garment structure. Move with deliberate, considered gestures and trust the styling even when the silhouette is extreme.

MUA & Hair

Create a conceptual, editorial beauty look that extends the garment idea rather than a conventional face. Build hair as a sculptural element with strong hold that can withstand the pose held for long takes.

Stylist

Engineer the look with rigging, tape and support so avant-garde pieces hold their shape on the body. Prioritise the concept and silhouette, and keep tools ready to reset structural elements between frames.

Pose & direction library
Poses & body
  1. Contort into an angular, architectural shape — elbows and knees as hard lines
  2. Elongate into an impossible-seeming stretch, one limb breaking the frame edge
  3. Fold forward from the hips, arms hanging, sculpture over face
  4. Twist the torso against the hips for a wrung, unnatural silhouette
  5. Frame the face with both hands in a stylized, mask-like gesture
  6. Perch high on a plinth or box, body as a single vertical statement
  7. Cross the arms hard across the chest, chin severe, negative space deliberate
  8. Recline in an unnatural diagonal, the garment sculptural over the body
  9. Point one arm rigid to a corner, gaze locked the opposite way
  10. Curl into a tight coiled ball, only the fabric structure reading
Expression & mimic
  • Blank, alien neutrality — face as pure form
  • Intense unblinking stare through the lens
  • Chin severely lifted, lids lowered, imperious
  • Lips sealed, jaw set, no human warmth
  • Eyes cast hard to one side, disconnected
  • Frozen, statuesque stillness held long
Directing cues
  • “Make a shape no body should make — hold it exactly.”
  • “Sharp elbows, sharp knees — think architecture.”
  • “Give me nothing on the face — you’re a sculpture.”
  • “Break the edge of frame with one arm — reach out.”
  • “Twist against yourself — wring the torso.”
  • “Freeze — don’t breathe the shape away.”
MUA & hair
  • Editorial concept makeup — graphic color-blocking or metallic planes
  • Reshaped or bleached brows for an otherworldly face
  • Sculptural hair — gelled architecture or an exaggerated form
  • Face gems, foil or negative-space liner for the concept
  • Bold matte lip in an unexpected shade to complete the statement

Accessories & Footwear — On Body

JEWELLERY · SKIN

On Skin

Key

3:1

A

Styling & Wardrobe

Rest a necklace on the collarbone or a ring on the hand so the jewellery meets warm skin. Clean every facet and set the piece so the metal and stone sit square to the light.

B

Lighting Micro-Adjustments

Use a strip box to draw a clean specular line along the metal and ignite the gemstone. A small silver card returns fill so the skin glows and the setting keeps detail.

C

Posing & Micro-Expressions

Hold the hand or neck still and relaxed so tendons soften and the jewellery sits natural. Rotate the piece a few degrees to catch the brightest facet in the focal plane.

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Shoot tight, considered crops that place the accessory or shoe on the body as the hero. Use directional light to define leather grain, metal and heel line, keeping focus precisely on the product.

Model

Present hands, wrists, neckline and feet with elegant, deliberate poise so the accessory reads clearly. Point the toe and angle the ankle to flatter footwear, and keep supporting body language quiet and clean.

MUA & Hair

Keep hands, nails and skin flawless and evenly toned since they frame the product in close crops. Style hair off the neckline and ears when jewellery is the hero so nothing competes with the piece.

Stylist

Keep footwear soles clean and accessories pristine, wiping fingerprints from metal and leather between takes. Style the surrounding wardrobe simply so the accessory stays the clear focal point.

Pose & direction library
Poses & body
  1. Rest the chin on the back of a ringed hand to feature the jewelry near the face
  2. Cross the legs seated and let a heeled foot lead the frame
  3. Sling a bag across the body, hand resting on the strap at the hip
  4. Lift a hand to the ear to showcase an earring, face turned in profile
  5. Point the toe on a step to elongate the leg and feature the shoe
  6. Drape a scarf and let both hands play with its ends near the collarbone
  7. Walk mid-stride so the bag swings and the shoes catch the light
  8. Perch on a ledge, ankles crossed, heels angled to camera
  9. Bring a sunglasses arm to the lips, elbow lifted, gaze over the frames
  10. Rest a bejeweled hand flat on the collarbone, fingers softly splayed
Expression & mimic
  • Soft downward gaze toward the featured accessory
  • Cool poised look over the top of sunglasses
  • Serene half-smile, chin turned to profile
  • Slow blink, lips just parted, elegant
  • Confident direct gaze while the hands work
  • Playful glance as the bag swings past
Directing cues
  • “Chin on your hand — let the ring sit right by your face.”
  • “Point the toe and lead with the shoe — long leg.”
  • “Touch your ear like you’re listening — profile to me.”
  • “Rest your hand on the strap, drop the hip.”
  • “Look over the frames — cool, unhurried.”
  • “Let the bag swing as you turn, then settle.”
MUA & hair
  • Flawless hands — buffed nails and moisturized skin for close ring shots
  • Polished neutral face that lets the product be the hero
  • Hair swept off the ears and neck to clear earrings and collars
  • Soft glow on the collarbone to flatter necklaces
  • A clean nude or classic red manicure to complement metals

Skincare Glow — Dewy Beauty

Skincare imagery has to look like health, not product, so every choice serves the impression of hydration and calm. We keep light soft and wrapping, protect true skin tone, and let a controlled dewiness read as the hero.

Colour

Retouch

Skin-Texture Hero

A macro study that celebrates real texture, dew and surface luminosity.

Detail crop

A

Styling & Textures

Apply a single fresh layer of serum right before capture for micro-droplet highlights. Keep the crop on the cheek or brow bone where texture is most beautiful.

B

Lighting Micro-Adjustments

Rake a soft close source across the skin to let each highlight catch dimensionally. Add a tight reflector to keep the shadow detail readable, not muddy.

C

Ask for absolute stillness and steady breathing to hold micro-focus. A relaxed muscle tone keeps the surface smooth and natural.

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Use soft, wrapping light that celebrates dewy, healthy skin and gives a clean glow to the highlights. Shoot close beauty crops with careful focus on the eyes and skin texture, avoiding harsh shadow.

Model

Relax the face and let the skin be the story, with soft, natural expressions and gentle eyes. Keep still for the tight focus and avoid touching the face so the dewy finish stays intact.

MUA & Hair

Build a luminous, hydrated base with strategic highlight so glow reads real rather than greasy under close light. Keep skin prep meticulous, exfoliated and moisturised, and style hair back to keep skin the hero.

Stylist

Keep wardrobe simple and skin-adjacent in soft neutral tones that support a dewy beauty focus. Choose clean necklines that frame the face and never distract from the glow.

Pose & direction library
Poses & body
  1. Tilt the face up into soft light to spread an even dewy sheen across the cheeks
  2. Press fingertips lightly to the cheekbone to suggest a skincare gesture
  3. Cup water to the face for a fresh, just-cleansed beauty frame
  4. Turn slowly to catch the highlight travelling across a glowing cheek
  5. Rest the chin lightly on the back of the hand, skin as the subject
  6. Sweep the hair fully off the face to bare a luminous complexion
  7. Close-crop the shoulders bare, chin lifted, neck long and dewy
  8. Lean toward the window light, forehead and cheek catching the glow
  9. Softly touch a drop of product to the cheek with one fingertip
  10. Angle three-quarter so the glow reads on the high plane of the cheek
Expression & mimic
  • Serene closed eyes, face bathed in soft light
  • Fresh, restful half-smile, skin relaxed
  • Slow blink with dewy, hydrated-looking lids
  • Lips softly parted on a calm breath
  • Gentle direct gaze, glowing and unforced
  • Eyes lifted to the light, wonder-soft
Directing cues
  • “Tip your face to the light — let it catch the glow.”
  • “Fingertips soft on your cheek — barely touch.”
  • “Breathe out, drop your shoulders — fresh and easy.”
  • “Close your eyes for me — feel the warmth.”
  • “Turn slow — I’m following the shine on your cheek.”
  • “Chin on your hand, skin does all the talking.”
MUA & hair
  • Skin-first prep — hydrate, prime and let real texture show
  • Sheer glow tint or balm instead of full coverage
  • Strategic dewy highlighter on cheekbones, brow bone and cupid’s bow
  • Clean fluffy brows and a slick of clear lash gloss
  • Hair pulled fully back so the complexion is the whole story

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Light cleanly and evenly to keep the pigment true, since colour accuracy is the whole point of the story. Shoot tight enough to showcase the makeup detail and confirm the hues on a calibrated monitor as you go.

Model

Give a neutral, open canvas with lifted brows and relaxed eyes so the colour reads without distortion. Hold precise eye positions on cue so graphic liner and shadow placement stay crisp in the frame.

MUA & Hair

Apply bold, saturated colour with clean crisp edges and dense pigment that photographs vividly. Keep the rest of the face controlled so the colour story stays the single hero, and style hair fully back off the face.

Stylist

Keep wardrobe tonal and simple so it supports rather than competes with the bold makeup palette. Choose necklines and colours that harmonise with the featured hue and keep the frame uncluttered.

Pose & direction library
Poses & body
  1. Close beauty frame, eyes cast down to showcase the lid color
  2. Turn to profile and drop the lids to feature a graphic liner wing
  3. Frame the lips with a fingertip to highlight a bold mouth
  4. Look straight to lens wide-eyed, brows lifted, lids fully visible
  5. Angle the face so a colored shadow catches raking light
  6. Rest the chin on stacked hands, eyes as the focal point
  7. Half-cover the face with a hand, only the made-up eye showing
  8. Tilt the head back slightly, chin up, to open the eye shape
  9. Press the lips together then release to show the pigment
  10. Sweep hair back and hold it, clearing the whole made-up face
Expression & mimic
  • Lids lowered to display the shadow, lashes down
  • Bold, confident stare with the mouth relaxed
  • Lips slightly parted to show the color and gloss
  • Slow blink revealing the full lid gradient
  • Chin up, eyes cool and direct for the color story
  • A knowing half-smile that keeps the lip shape crisp
Directing cues
  • “Look down slow — show me the whole lid.”
  • “Chin up, eyes to me — let the color pop.”
  • “Press your lips, then part them just a little.”
  • “Turn to profile — I want the wing sharp.”
  • “Big confident eyes — the color’s the star.”

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Backlight and rim-light the hair to make shine and movement pop against a clean background. Shoot fast to freeze the flick and swing, and time bursts to the peak of each hair toss.

Model

Deliver controlled hair movement, tosses, turns and flicks, on cue and repeatable for the camera. Keep your face composed and posture tall as the hair moves so the frame stays elegant.

MUA & Hair

Prep hair for maximum shine and healthy movement with polish and lightweight product, avoiding stiffness. Keep makeup clean and supporting so all attention stays on the hair, and reset the style between tosses.

Stylist

Choose necklines and colours that frame the hair and let it fall unobstructed against the wardrobe. Keep shoulders clean and clothing simple so nothing catches or hides the moving hair.

Pose & direction library
Poses & body
  1. Whip the head so the hair fans into a full arc mid-frame

  5. Flip forward then snap upright for a big-volume freeze
  6. Sweep the hair to one side and hold it in a cascade down the arm
  7. Face away and glance back so the hair sweeps across the frame
  8. Sit tall and let long hair fall in a straight shining sheet
  9. Shake out loose waves with a light hand-scrunch mid-motion
  10. Lift a section to camera to feature length, ends and shine

Jewelry — Macro Sparkle

Fine jewelry lives or dies on the quality of its highlights, so every surface in the set exists to shape light before it ever reaches metal or stone. We build reflections deliberately, favouring one clean specular event over a chaos of stray glints.

ProductJewelryHeroDetailLifestyle

Baseline — Jewelry

Surface

Black acrylic gives a controlled mirror pool beneath the piece for depth.

Scale

Focus stacking is mandatory at true macro to hold facet-to-clasp sharpness.

Cleanliness

Dust and fingerprints are retouch time, so we glove up and blow off every shot.

A

Set & Surface

Lay the piece on clean black acrylic and tilt it a few degrees so the reflection reads as a pool rather than a hard mirror. Keep the background falling to true black so the metal edge separates cleanly.

B

Lighting Micro-Adjustments

Feed a large gradient scrim overhead so the metal picks up a long, graduated highlight instead of a hotspot. Flag both sides with black cards to carve crisp specular edges and add dimension.

C

Composition & Camera

Shoot slightly above eye level so the reflection has room to breathe under the piece. Stack twelve frames from front facet to rear clasp to hold edge-to-edge sharpness at f/11.

Set & Surface

Nestle the stone on a matte grey riser so nothing competes with the fire. Keep surrounding surfaces neutral so the only bright events are the facets themselves.

B

Bring one small hard pinlight in from high camera-left to ignite the facets, then feather a silver bounce underneath to lift the pavilion. Dim the key until the metal holds detail and the stone still throws colour.

Push to 1.5x macro and stack eighteen frames to keep the entire crown crisp. Nudge the pinlight a degree at a time between test frames until the fire pattern peaks.

B

Wrap a medium softbox from the side to model the skin and give the metal a soft rolling highlight. Fill with a white bounce opposite to keep shadow density gentle and flattering.

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Shoot macro with controlled pinpoint light to make gemstones spark while holding metal detail without blowout. Focus-stack for full sharpness across the piece and manage every reflection on the polished surfaces.

Prop Stylist

Choose refined surfaces and risers, velvet, stone or acrylic, that flatter the metal and stone tones. Position each piece to show its best facet and keep chains and settings elegantly arranged.

Set & Assist

Rig precise reflectors, flags and tweezers to place catchlights on each stone at macro distance. Keep the set dust-free and steady, since any speck or vibration ruins a sparkle frame.

Retoucher

Clean dust and stray reflections while preserving genuine gemstone brilliance and metal character. Enhance the sparkle tastefully and keep proportions and colour of the piece true.

Styling & angle library
Arrangements
  1. Single hero ring on black velvet, one facet throwing a controlled star of light
  2. Nested necklace coil with the clasp hidden and the pendant leading
  3. Stacked bangles graduated by diameter for a rhythmic macro line
  4. Earrings paired in gentle mirror symmetry on a reflective riser
  5. Loose gemstones scattered in a shallow arc to show cut variety
  6. Ring balanced upright in a clear acrylic stand for a floating look
  7. Chain drawn in a soft S-curve across a raked-light surface
  8. Grouped set — ring, pendant, studs — in a tight family cluster
Hero angles
  • Straight-on macro at the table facet to maximize fire and sparkle
  • Slight top-down three-quarter to read the full stone setting
  • Extreme macro on the prongs and pave detail
  • Low angle catching the stone against a dark gradient
  • Profile of the band to show the gallery and side stones
Prop & set styling
  • Black or deep-jewel velvet to sink the background and lift the metal
  • A single acrylic riser to float the piece off the surface
  • Water droplets or a fine mist for a fresh, dewy sparkle
  • Torn silk or a marble slab for a luxe editorial base
  • Mirror tile beneath for a clean symmetrical reflection
Finish & retouch
  • Dust-map and clean every facet at 100% before delivery
  • Enhance the diamond fire while keeping the sparkle believable
  • Even the metal reflections and kill stray hotspots
  • Focus-stack the macro for edge-to-edge sharp facets

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Shoot flat top-down with even, shadow-controlled light so every item reads sharp across the grid. Lock the camera on a copy stand and keep the horizon square for clean alignment.

Prop Stylist

Arrange items on precise grid lines with consistent spacing and parallel edges for satisfying knolling. Balance colour, scale and negative space so the composition reads deliberate and clean.

Set & Assist

Align each object with a level and guides and use museum putty to hold pieces exactly in place. Keep the surface and every item dust-free since flat light shows all debris.

Retoucher

Straighten and align the grid precisely, cleaning dust and stray shadow while keeping items true. Even out tone and spacing so the final knoll reads crisp and orderly.

Styling & angle library
Arrangements
  1. Knoll every item on a strict grid, edges parallel and evenly gapped
  2. Group by category into tidy clusters within the layout
  3. Order by size, largest anchor to smallest accent, for visual rhythm
  4. Center a hero piece and radiate supporting items around it
  5. Color-block the objects into a graded spectrum across the frame
  6. Leave generous negative space so each item breathes
  7. Align all handles, spouts and text to a single direction
  8. Build a diagonal flow of items for a dynamic flat lay variant
Hero angles
  • Perfect nadir top-down, camera dead level to the surface
  • Slight three-quarter overhead for an editorial flat-lay variant
  • Macro pass on a single hero item within the grid
  • Corner-to-corner tight crop to emphasize the grid rhythm
  • Straight-down detail on aligned edges and gaps
Prop & set styling
  • Seamless flat backdrop — paper, stone or wood — lint-free
  • Overhead soft light for even, shadow-controlled illumination
  • Hidden museum putty to keep round items from rolling
  • A gridded guide or tape marks off-frame for precise alignment
  • A cohesive prop palette so nothing breaks the color story
Finish & retouch
  • Straighten the frame and true every edge to horizontal and vertical
  • Even gaps and nudge items into perfect alignment
  • Clean dust and stray fibers from the whole surface
  • Balance shadows for a clean, consistent flat-lay light
  • True colors across all items so the palette reads unified

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Backlight the glass to make the liquid glow and freeze the pour with flash duration, not just shutter. Pre-focus on the stream, shoot in bursts, and keep a locked tripod so you can composite the cleanest pour later.

Food Stylist

Chill and polish the glass, use fresh product per take and manage condensation with glycerine so beads read as fresh, not sweaty. Have backups poured and ready so momentum never drops between resets.

Set & Assist

Protect the floor and gear with towels and trays and keep a stack of dry glasses queued for rapid swaps. Steady the pour to a repeatable height and rhythm so every frame is usable.

Retoucher

Composite the strongest pour shape, clean stray splashes and even out the highlight running down the glass. Keep the liquid colour appetising and true to her product without going artificially saturated.

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Rake soft directional light across the cut surface to reveal crumb, flake and layer texture. Shoot the cross-section fast and focus-stack if needed so every layer stays sharp.

Food Stylist

Cut with a warm serrated blade for clean crumb, dust sugar last and place stray flakes deliberately. Work quickly on the hero slice before butter softens or icing slumps under the lights.

Set & Assist

Keep a chilled backup batch off-set and blow away loose crumbs between frames with a soft puffer. Steady tweezed placements and mark the plate position for consistent resets.

Retoucher

Enhance crumb and flake micro-contrast without turning it gritty, and clean stray sugar where it distracts. Warm the bake tones to golden and keep her product looking fresh from the oven.

Splash & Action — Dynamic

Action food photography turns a static product into a frozen moment, a splash suspended, a drop crowning, a garnish caught mid-toss. We use short strobe duration and dark backlit fields to carve motion out of time.

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Freeze motion with short flash duration and backlight the splash so droplets read crisp against a dark falloff. Pre-focus, trigger in bursts, and lock the frame to composite the best splash shape.

Food Stylist

Prep fresh product and props per take and manage the drop height for a repeatable, photogenic splash. Keep backups queued so the crew can fire take after take without losing energy.

Set & Assist

Waterproof the floor and gear, keep towels and a tray under the action, and dry the set between frames. Deliver the drop or splash on a steady cue so timing stays predictable.

Retoucher

Composite the strongest droplets, remove stray splatter and tidy the rim of the splash crown. Keep the liquid and product colour true and appetising while preserving the sense of motion.

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Keep the room warm, work slowly and shoot soft directional window light with the baby always supported. Never rush a pose; capture the small, quiet moments and let safety lead every frame over the shot list.

Subject & Guardians

Guide mum to stay close and hands-on so the newborn feels secure and settled throughout. Encourage feeding and soothing breaks whenever needed, and reassure her that fussiness is normal and welcome.

MUA & Hair

Keep any touch-ups on mum gentle, hypoallergenic and fragrance-light near the baby. Offer soft, natural finishing so she feels lovely without heavy product close to the infant.

Stylist

Choose soft, breathable, seam-friendly wraps and neutral tones that flatter mum and baby together. Have layers pre-warmed and easy to change, prioritising the baby comfort at every swap.

  8. Wrapped potato-sack upright against mum’s shoulder
  9. Tiny-details macro — lashes, fingers, toes — while settled
  10. Sibling gently resting a hand beside, never over, the baby

  • Wait for the natural newborn stretch & yawn
  • Soft pursed-lip dreaming expression
  • Fleeting wide-eyed calm-awake moment
  • Mother gazing down, tender & unposed
  • Sibling’s awed, gentle curiosity
Directing cues
  • “Keep a hand on baby the whole time — I’ll blend it out later.”
  • “Let’s wait for the deep sleep before we shape anything.”
  • “Warm your hands first, then bring them in slowly.”
  • “Look down at your little one, forget the camera.”
  • “Whisper to baby — that softness reaches your face.”
  • “If baby stirs, we pause — comfort always comes first.”
MUA & hair

  • Hair pinned back so it never brushes the newborn
  • Gentle under-eye brighten for tired new parents
  • Neutral, hypoallergenic product choices only
  • Soft loose waves for a timeless heirloom feel

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Get down to the pet eye level and shoot fast, patient bursts to catch the bond and fleeting expressions. Keep the pace calm and let the animal set the tempo so both subjects stay relaxed and safe.

Subject & Handler

MUA & Hair

Stylist

Choose fur-friendly tones and textures that hide hair and flatter her with the pet. Keep a lint roller and backups ready and avoid dangling pieces the animal will grab.

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Compose her against the vista with scale, using the light and layered ridgelines for depth. Work efficiently as mountain weather and light shift fast, and mind edges and footing when placing her.

Model

Guide open, expansive poses that celebrate the view while she stays safely back from drop-offs. Keep her warm between frames and watch for wind gusts on exposed ground.

MUA & Hair

Keep a fresh, weather-resistant finish and pack layers for cold, thin-air conditions. Use strong hold to fight altitude wind and refresh quickly between climbs.

Stylist

Choose bold, wind-worthy pieces in tones that pop against grey rock and sky. Bring warm layers and secure loose fabric so silhouettes stay clean at altitude.

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Backlight the rain so droplets sparkle and protect the camera with rain covers and lens cloths. Raise shutter to freeze streaks and shoot fast to keep gear and crew safe and dry between takes.

Model

Coach her to embrace the wet for cinematic emotion while keeping her warm and safe from chills. Mind slippery footing and give her frequent breaks under cover to reset.

MUA & Hair

Go fully waterproof and lean into a sleek, wet-look styling that suits the rain. Keep towels and warm layers ready and refresh her fast between exposures.

Stylist

Choose fabrics that look intentional and flattering when soaked, avoiding transparency issues. Have dry backups, towels and a warm robe on standby for every reset.

Vol. 70Craft · Atmosphere

Smoke & Haze — Atmosphere

Atmosphere is not decoration; it is the medium that makes a light beam visible and gives depth a physical body. We build haze in controlled layers so the air reads as intentional volume rather than accidental fog.

IntermediateKit 1–2 lights + a modifier
CraftAtmosphereBACKLIT GLOWGOD-RAYSCOLOURED SMOKE

RelatedFragrance — The Sensory · Water & Splash — The Rig · Levitation & Composite — The Trick

Baseline — ATMOSPHERE

Air Control

Seal the room, kill HVAC drafts, and let haze settle to an even bed before the first frame.

Backlight First

Position the strongest source behind or across the subject so particles catch and glow.

Ventilation Plan

Water-based haze only, with breaks and airway awareness for anyone with respiratory sensitivity.

Capture

85mm f/1.4 · 1/200 f/2.8 ISO 400.

Starting exposureManual · 1/160 sync · f/8 · ISO 100 · WB 5200KShutter controls ambient only — flash power sets the exposure. Sync tops out near 1/200; switch to HSS for 1/250 and up.

BACKLIT GLOW

Backlit Haze Glow

A soft luminous halo separates the subject from a dissolving background.

Haze
Light bed
Key

Ratio

85mm
A

Set & Instrument

Lay a thin, even haze bed and place a gridded strip behind the subject aimed toward camera. Keep the hero face lit by a soft frontal source so features stay clean while the air glows.

B

Lighting Micro-Adjustments

Feather the backlight so its core misses the lens and only the halo remains. Add or subtract a single puff of haze to tune glow density rather than dimming the source.

C

Read & Faults

Watch for lens flare veiling and use a flag or matte box to protect the front element. Uneven haze streaks read as smudges, so let the room settle between takes.

02
GOD-RAYS

Shafts & God-Rays

Hard collimated beams cut through haze to build dramatic diagonal architecture.

Haze
Medium
Key
Hard top
Gobo
Slats
BG
Dark
Lens
85mm
A

Set & Instrument

Fire a hard-edged fresnel or optical spot through a slatted gobo to carve defined shafts. A denser haze bed gives the beams body without swallowing the whole frame.

B

Lighting Micro-Adjustments

Angle the source steeply so rays rake across the subject rather than blowing out the face. Adjust gobo distance to sharpen or soften the edge of each shaft.

C

Read & Faults

Too much haze flattens the rays into a milky wash, so build density gradually. Confirm the subject still has a clean fill so eyes do not fall into shadow.

03
COLOURED SMOKE

Coloured Smoke

Gelled sources tint drifting smoke into saturated bands of mood.

Media
Smoke
Key
Gelled rim
Gel
Dual tone
BG
Dark
Lens
85mm
A

Set & Instrument

Use a controlled smoke source and gel two rim lights in complementary hues so the drift picks up colour edges. Keep a neutral or gently warm key on the face for skin fidelity.

B

Lighting Micro-Adjustments

Balance the two gels so neither dominates and the smoke transitions cleanly between tones. Cut smoke volume before adding light, since dense colour quickly turns muddy.

C

Read & Faults

Coloured spill on skin looks sickly, so flag rim gels off the face. Ventilate between bursts and avoid pyrotechnic smoke indoors in favour of safe fluid haze.

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Backlight the haze to shape volumetric beams and meter for the atmosphere, not just the subject. Fire the machine in controlled bursts and let it settle so density reads even across frames.

Model

Keep her posing calm and give clean-air breaks so the haze never irritates her eyes or throat. Cue her to hold still as atmosphere settles so the beams stay defined around her.

MUA & Hair

Use a finish that holds in warm, humid haze and refresh between fills. Watch that product does not smudge as atmosphere condenses on the skin.

Stylist

Choose fabrics that catch backlight and beams without collecting a damp sheen. Keep the set ventilated between takes so wardrobe does not absorb odour or moisture.

Water & Splash — The Rig

Water photography lives or dies on the rig behind the frame, where timing, containment and gear protection matter as much as light. We treat every splash as an engineered event with a dry electrical path and a rehearsed cue.

Gear Protection

Rain covers on bodies, splash bags on strobes, and GFCI protection on every mains circuit.

Freeze Duration

Short flash duration on a fast-recycling pack captures crisp droplets.

Containment

Tarps, drains and towels so water stays where the shot needs it.

Set & Instrument

Mist the subject with a fine spray and add a hard rim to pick out wet highlights on skin and hair. For tank or pool work, use a housing and keep an assistant spotting for safety at all times.

B

Lighting Micro-Adjustments

Control specular hotspots with a large soft key so wet skin glows without blowing out. Reapply mist frequently, since water dries and flattens the look between frames.

Overspray causes lens droplets, so shield the front element and wipe often. Keep water temperature comfortable and limit submersion time to protect the subject.

Set & Instrument

Suspend a plumbed rain bar overhead and light it from behind so the falling streaks catch the light. Contain runoff with a tarped basin and route all cabling away from the wet floor.

B

Lighting Micro-Adjustments

A backlight or hard rim renders rain as bright streaks against the dark background. Adjust flow rate to tune between fine drizzle and heavy downpour without soaking the front light.

Read & Faults

Frontal fill kills rain visibility, so keep fill low and let backlight carry the water. Watch footing on wet surfaces and provide warm towels and breaks between setups.

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Freeze the water with short flash duration and backlight it for crisp, sparkling droplets. Keep electrics GFCI-protected and gear shielded, and lock the frame to composite the best splash.

Model

Direct her through the splash while keeping her warm, safe-footed and free to call breaks. Warn her before each hit so she can brace and keep expressions controlled.

MUA & Hair

Go waterproof and plan a deliberate wet-look that survives repeated soakings. Keep towels, robe and warm-ups ready to reset her fast between takes.

Stylist

Choose fabrics that flatter wet and stay opaque, with dry backups on rotation. Manage slip hazards and keep the crew area toweled and safe around the rig.

  8. Hands cupping & releasing water mid-frame
  9. Walk through spray toward camera
  10. Still hero with droplets suspended around her

Support the subject on a rated stool or rigging positioned to be paintable-out later. Lock the camera on a tripod and note every setting so the clean plate matches exactly.

Lighting Micro-Adjustments

Fix the key and fill positions and do not touch them between the hero and clean-plate frames. Keep shadows on the floor consistent so the removed support leaves no lighting gap.

Any camera drift breaks the composite, so use a remote release and a stable floor. Ensure the support is genuinely load-rated and the subject is spotted while posed.

Set & Instrument

Shoot each element (subject, props, environment) as its own plate against the same locked camera. Keep a shot list and slate each plate so the composite stage stays organised.

B

Lighting Micro-Adjustments

Match light direction, quality and colour temperature across every plate. Photograph a grey and colour reference in each setup so grading can normalise them later.

C

Mismatched perspective or scale betrays the trick, so keep lens and distance constant. Shadow direction that disagrees between plates is the most common giveaway.

Set & Instrument

After the hero frame, clear the subject and support and shoot the empty scene with identical settings. This clean plate becomes the source for painting out rigging cleanly.

B

Lighting Micro-Adjustments

Do not adjust a single light or the tripod between hero and clean plate. Even a small exposure shift forces awkward blending, so lock everything down first.

C

Read & Faults

People stepping into frame or bumping stands ruins the plate, so guard the set. Verify focus and framing on the clean plate before releasing the setup.

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Lock the camera on a sturdy tripod and shoot matched plates for support rig and clean background. Keep lighting and focus identical across frames so the levitation composite is seamless.

Model

Support her fully on an apple box or rig and never ask for an unsafe hold. Coach a relaxed, weightless expression and pose while she is properly and comfortably braced.

MUA & Hair

Style hair and fabric to suggest float, pinning or supporting pieces for the composite. Keep the look consistent between the support and clean plates.

Stylist

Choose garments that drape convincingly as if suspended and hide any rigging. Keep wardrobe identical across plates so the trick holds together in post.

Place a pane of glass in front of the lens and let controlled reflections of lights or objects overlay the subject. Position the reflected elements deliberately so the layer supports rather than clutters.

Set & Instrument

Light so the reflection retains enough tone to read without competing with the subject. A calm, undisturbed surface gives the cleanest mirror, so let ripples settle.

Ripples and debris break the illusion, so filter the water and shield it from drafts. Protect cabling and footing around any water tray as with all wet setups.

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Work the mirror angles deliberately so reflections build layers without catching you or the rig. Manage focus between subject and reflection and flag stray light bouncing off the glass.

Model

Guide her placement so real and reflected poses both read cleanly, minding sharp mirror edges. Keep her movements controlled around glass and give clear cues for each layered position.

MUA & Hair

Ensure the look reads flawlessly from every reflected angle, not just to camera. Keep both profiles refined since the mirror shows what a single view would hide.

Stylist

Style so the outfit works front and reflected, with no distracting tags or pins visible. Keep mirrors spotless and handle glass safely during resets.

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Shoot at the child’s eye level with a fast shutter and continuous burst so genuine giggles and mid-jump moments stay sharp. Keep the session short and game-led, letting the tween lead the play while you follow rather than pose.

Model

Encourage the young client to move, spin and be silly between frames so real energy replaces stiff smiles. Reassure her that there is no wrong way to play, and let a favourite toy or friend ease any first-frame nerves.

MUA & Hair

Keep skin bare and hair natural with only light flyaway control, since a made-up look reads wrong on a child. Have a comb and clip ready for quick between-shot tidies without ever slowing the play.

Stylist

Choose playful, well-fitting kidswear in bright blocks that photograph clean and let her move freely. Pin any loose waistbands from behind and keep a backup outfit ready for the inevitable spill.

  8. On tiptoe reaching up for a balloon string
  9. Curled up hugging a favourite soft toy
  10. Skipping sideways across frame, one foot lifted

  • Fake-serious pout that breaks into a smile
  • Surprised gasp, hands to cheeks

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Build the frame around a single tone, watching how light falls across matching garment and backdrop to keep separation through shape and shadow rather than colour. Meter carefully so the one hue holds detail and never blocks up or blows out.

Model

Let posture and line carry the image, since a monochrome frame rewards strong, deliberate shapes over expression. Hold each pose a beat longer so the stylist can read the silhouette against the matched ground.

MUA & Hair

Match makeup temperature to the chosen tone so the face sits within the palette rather than fighting it. Keep hair sculpted and clean-edged so it reads as form, not distraction, against the single colour.

Stylist

Source every layer within one tonal family and play texture against texture to keep a same-colour look from going flat. Tape and pin for crisp lines, because in monochrome every wrinkle becomes the only visible event.

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Drag the shutter and add a touch of rear-curtain flash so the body streaks while an anchor point stays crisp. Rehearse the movement path first so the sweep resolves into intention rather than mush.

Model

Move on a repeatable count so the blur lands the same way each take, keeping one feature such as the eyes still at the flash. Commit fully to the gesture, because a timid sweep reads as a mistake rather than motion.

MUA & Hair

Set makeup to stay put through repeated dynamic takes and keep colours bold enough to survive the streak. Style hair so it moves cleanly and creates its own graceful trail through the frame.

Stylist

Choose fabrics with flow and weight that paint pleasing arcs as she moves, avoiding stiff pieces that stay static. Secure fastenings so nothing flies open mid-sweep and ruins an otherwise perfect trail.

Poses & body

  2. Fast spin with the skirt trailing a blur arc
  3. Hair whipped side to side on a head turn
  4. Sleeve or scarf flung to streak across frame
  5. Sudden lunge forward, torso sharp and still
  6. Twirl with arms out to smear the limbs
  7. Head still, hands sweeping fast past the face
  8. Skipping across so the feet ghost the floor
  9. Dress lifted and dropped for a falling-fabric blur
  10. Cross-frame dash, face held level and calm
Expression & mimic
  • Calm face anchored while the body streaks
  • Eyes locked on lens through the motion
  • Serene closed-eye during the sweep
  • Confident half-smile held steady
  • Chin lifted, unbothered by the movement
  • Soft neutral, no tension in the jaw
Directing cues
  • “Keep your face still while the dress flies”
  • “Move on three, then hold your eyes on me”
  • “Big sweep of the arm, but soft, not stiff”
  • “Walk at me like the shutter isn’t there”
  • “Let the fabric do the running, you stay steady”
  • “One turn, all the way through, don’t stop short”
MUA & hair
  • Loose flowing hair reads best in the sweep
  • Lock skin makeup so sweat under lights holds
  • Add a light-catching sheen for blur trails
  • Avoid loose pins that fly out mid-motion
  • Bold defined lip stays crisp against the blur

On-set crew brief

Stylist

Use high-CRI light and set a custom white balance off a grey card. Keep fill the same colour temperature so undertone stays consistent across the face.

C

Posing & Micro-Expressions

Favour a clean three-quarter angle that shows even skin across both planes. Keep the expression relaxed and true so the portrait feels authentic.

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Expose for the skin in front of you rather than a single default, adjusting so every tone renders true and richly detailed. Use a neutral reference and consistent light so no complexion is flattened or shifted in the edit.

Model

Bring your natural undertone forward with confidence, knowing the whole setup is built to honour it faithfully. Relax into the light so the portrait reads as you, not a corrected version of you.

MUA & Hair

Match foundation and finish precisely to her true depth and undertone, never lightening or greying the complexion. Choose products that keep the skin luminous and accurate under the shoot lights across every setup.

Stylist

Select colours that flatter and celebrate her specific skin tone rather than fighting it. Test wardrobe against the light early so nothing casts an unflattering colour onto true skin.

Pose & direction library
Poses & body
  1. Face lifted into even soft light, chin level
  2. Hand framing one cheek to show skin depth
  3. Three-quarter turn catching a gentle highlight
  4. Shoulders bare, neck long, gaze direct
  5. Fingertips resting at the collarbone
  6. Slow head tilt following the key light
  7. Both hands cradling the jawline
  8. Profile against a complementary backdrop
  9. Eyes closed, face tipped to the source
  10. Straight-on symmetry, relaxed open posture
Expression & mimic
  • Confident calm gaze into the lens
  • Soft proud half-smile
  • Serene closed eyes, jaw loose
  • Warm open expression, brows relaxed
  • Quiet strength, chin lifted
  • Gentle knowing smile
Directing cues
  • “Turn until the light loves your skin, then hold”
  • “Give me your face, honest and unhurried”
  • “Soften your eyes, let the real you sit there”
  • “Lift your chin a touch, own the frame”
  • “Breathe out and let your shoulders settle”
  • “Look at me like you’ve nothing to prove”
MUA & hair
  • Match foundation to the neck and chest exactly
  • Use undertone-correct shades, never one-size base
  • Balance highlight so no tone reads ashy or grey
  • Choose lip and blush that flatter the undertone
  • Keep hair off the face to let skin lead

Stylist

Photographer

Build clean, gradient reflections on glass and metal using large soft sources and careful flag control to shape the glow. Shoot tethered and check screens at full zoom so every edge stays crisp and every reflection intentional.

Prop Stylist

Set & Assist

Retoucher

Clean residual dust, unify the reflection gradients and keep screen content crisp and colour-accurate. Preserve the true material finish so the retouch reads as flawless product, not plastic render.

Set & Assist

Retoucher

Photographer

Stylist

Vol. 96Creative · Multiple Exposure

Double Exposure — Layered Frames

Double exposure is composition across time: a portrait and a second frame occupying the same negative space. The craft is in choosing which tones survive the blend and protecting the subject from becoming noise.

AdvancedKit Tripod + creative tools
CreativeMultiple ExposureIn-camera blendSilhouette fillMask & blend

RelatedLight Painting — Drawn Light · Shadow Play — Pattern & Form · Long Exposure — Motion & Trails

Baseline — Layered Frames

Base tone

Keep the portrait low-key so bright textures read in the shadow side.

Second frame

Choose high-contrast texture that resolves cleanly against skin.

Alignment

Place detail over the darker half of the face, not the eyes.

Capture

50mm f/1.8 · ISO 100 · in-camera multiple exposure, additive blend.

Starting exposureManual · 1/160 sync · f/8 · ISO 100 · WB 5200KShutter controls ambient only — flash power sets the exposure. Sync tops out near 1/200; switch to HSS for 1/250 and up.
01

Mode
Multi-exp additive
Base
Low-key portrait

Bark / stone

100

50mm f/1.8

Set & Instrument

Shoot the portrait first against black so the shadow side stays empty for the layer. Meter the second frame a stop under to keep highlights from blowing the face.

B

Lighting Micro-Adjustments

Feather the key off the far cheek to hold a broad dark zone that will carry texture. Add a whisper of rim so the head still separates once layered.

C

Read & Faults

If texture crosses the eyes the image reads as damage, not design; recompose. Watch for muddy midtones where two mid-bright areas overlap and dull each other.

Foliage Within

Base

Fill
Backlit leaves
Blend
Bright base
