100
Lens
85mm f/2
A

Set & Instrument

Expose the profile as a hard silhouette against a bright wall so the body becomes a dark mask. In additive mode the second frame only fills that mask, so the outline must be clean-edged.

B

Lighting Micro-Adjustments

Light the foliage frame evenly and slightly over to push detail into the silhouette. Keep the surrounding background of frame two dark so it does not fog the bright base.

C

Read & Faults

A soft silhouette edge lets foliage spill past the body and breaks the illusion. If the fill looks flat, add contrast to frame two before blending, not after.

03
Mask & blend

Post Composite

Combine two exposures with a mask for precise control.

Frames
Two RAW
Blend
Screen / lighten
Mask
Luminosity
ISO
100
Lens
50mm f/1.8
A

Set & Instrument

Shoot both frames on a tripod at matched focal length so scale and edges stay consistent. A luminosity mask lets you protect the eyes and mouth while texture flows over the rest.

B

Lighting Micro-Adjustments

Grade both layers to a shared colour temperature so the composite feels lit by one source. Dodge the texture back off the catchlights to keep the gaze alive.

C

Read & Faults

Screen blends can grey the blacks; a levels tweak on the mask restores depth. If the join looks pasted, feather the mask edge and lower texture opacity near the face.

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Plan the two layers deliberately, shooting a clean silhouette against dark to blend with a textured second frame. Meter both exposures so the composite holds detail, and keep the layering intentional rather than muddy.

Model

Give a strong, clean profile or shape for the base layer, holding still so the outline stays crisp for blending. Understand your silhouette becomes the vessel, so posture and edge matter more than expression.

MUA & Hair

Keep the base look clean-edged so the silhouette reads sharp where the second exposure fills it. Style hair with a defined outline that blends gracefully rather than tangling the layered frame.

Stylist

Choose simple, strong shapes that make a clear silhouette for the layering to inhabit. Avoid busy patterns on the base layer so the second exposure has room to show through cleanly.

Vol. 97Creative · Light Painting

Light Painting — Drawn Light

Light painting adds a mark-making layer to portraiture: the subject holds still while you draw with a moving source over seconds. Success is a matter of rhythm, wardrobe safety, and reading the histogram between takes.

AdvancedKit Tripod + creative tools
CreativeLight PaintingLight trailsPainted rimColoured strokes

RelatedDouble Exposure — Layered Frames · Shadow Play — Pattern & Form · Long Exposure — Motion & Trails

Baseline — Drawn Light

Stillness

Brace the pose or seat the subject so a long exposure stays sharp.

Ambient

Kill room light so only your drawn light registers.

Tool

Use an LED wand or fibre and keep it away from skin and hair.

Capture

35mm f/8 · ISO 100 · 6-15s · tripod, remote release.

Starting exposureManual / Bulb · 1/15 to 30s · f/8–f/11 · ISO 100 · tripodDarken the room and drag the shutter or open on Bulb. Lock the camera down, shoot many, and check the trails at 100%.
01
Light trails

Orbiting Light

Wrap streaks of light around a static figure.

Shutter
8-12s
Aperture
f/8
ISO
100
Tool
LED wand
Flash
Rear-curtain pop
A

Set & Instrument

Seat the subject and add one gentle flash pop to freeze the face while the shutter stays open. Walk a wand in a wide arc behind and beside them, keeping the source pointed away from the lens.

B

Lighting Micro-Adjustments

Set flash to rear-curtain so the sharp portrait lands after the trails, not before. Dim the wand or speed your walk if trails clip to pure white.

C

Read & Faults

Ghosting on the subject means they moved; brace shoulders and shorten the exposure. Trails crossing the face read as clutter, so keep your arc behind the head.

02
Painted rim

Hand-Drawn Edge

Rim the hair and shoulder by hand with a small wand.

Shutter
6-8s
Aperture
f/8
ISO
100
Tool
Pen light
Move
Behind subject
A

Set & Instrument

Stand behind the subject and skim a pen light down the hairline and shoulder to draw a controlled rim. Keep your body hidden by theirs so you do not record as a shadow.

B

Lighting Micro-Adjustments

Feather the light so it grazes rather than points, giving a soft edge instead of a hot line. One slow pass usually beats several nervous strokes.

C

Read & Faults

A jagged rim betrays a shaky hand; steady your elbow against your side. If the wand shows in frame, you overshot the edge and should tighten the pass.

03
Coloured strokes

Motion in Colour

Layer coloured light strokes as graphic motion.

Shutter
10-15s
Aperture
f/8
ISO
100
Tool
RGB wand
Gels
Two colours
A

Set & Instrument

Plan two or three gestures in colours that complement wardrobe, and rehearse them before opening the shutter. Freeze the subject with a low flash pop so the strokes float around a sharp figure.

B

Lighting Micro-Adjustments

Balance stroke brightness by matching wand speed to each colour, since some LEDs read hotter. Leave a dark gap between strokes and skin so colour does not stain the face.

C

Read & Faults

Too many strokes turn the frame to soup; three deliberate marks beat a dozen. If colours muddy where they cross, separate them in space or in successive frames.

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Work in near-darkness with a long exposure, drawing light trails around her while a brief flash freezes the pose sharp. Keep the tripod locked and the frame planned so the drawn light lands as intended each pass.

Model

Hold your pose perfectly still through the whole exposure so you stay sharp while the light moves around you. Trust the routine and stay patient in the dark, keeping breathing shallow so nothing blurs.

MUA & Hair

Set a look that reads under the brief flash, keeping definition that survives a single frozen burst. Fix hair securely so the held pose stays clean through every long, still exposure.

Stylist

Dress in pieces that hold their line while she stays still and read cleanly under the freezing flash. Keep the safety of light sources and dark-set movement in mind, taping cables and clearing her path between takes.

Baseline — Pattern & Form

Hard source

Use a small, undiffused light so the shadow edge stays crisp.

Distance

Move the gobo closer to the subject for sharper pattern.

Placement

Let the pattern lead the eye toward, not across, the eyes.

Capture

85mm f/4 · ISO 200 · single hard source, black flags.

01
Gobo pattern

Cut on Skin

Throw a hard gobo pattern across the face and shoulder.

Source
Bare / optical
Gobo
Cut card
Aperture
f/4
ISO
200
Angle
45 degrees
A

Set & Instrument

Place a cut card or optical gobo between a hard source and the subject to project a defined shape. Slide the card toward the face to sharpen the edge and away to soften it.

B

Lighting Micro-Adjustments

Angle the source so the pattern rakes across form and reveals cheekbone and jaw. Add a low negative fill on the shadow side to keep the cut crisp.

C

Read & Faults

A pattern flat across both eyes hides expression; drop it below the brow line. If the edge is mushy, the source is too large or the gobo too far away.

02
Venetian stripes

Blinds & Bars

Stripe the subject with venetian-blind bars.

Source
Hard, off-axis
Gobo
Blind slats
Aperture
f/4
ISO
200
Bars
Diagonal
A

Set & Instrument

Rig a real or faux venetian blind between the light and subject for parallel bars. Tilt the slats to run the stripes diagonally, which flatters the figure more than dead-level lines.

B

Lighting Micro-Adjustments

Adjust slat spacing so a bright bar lands on the eyes and the gaze survives. Keep the source small and far for even, parallel stripes rather than fanned ones.

C

Read & Faults

Converging bars mean the source is too close; back it off. A stripe splitting the mouth reads as an accident, so shift the subject a few centimetres.

03
Organic cast

Foliage & Lace

Dapple the subject with foliage or lace shadow.

Source
Hard, single
Gobo
Leaves / lace
Aperture
f/4
ISO
200
Cast
Soft dapple
A

Set & Instrument

Hang a branch or lace panel in the beam for an organic, irregular cast. Rotate the material slightly between frames to find a pattern that frames rather than clutters the face.

B

Lighting Micro-Adjustments

Balance sharpness by distance so the dapple reads without becoming a busy scramble. A faint negative fill keeps the lit gaps luminous against the shadow.

C

Read & Faults

Overlapping leaf shadows can erase the eyes entirely; open a clean pool of light for the face. If it looks random, simplify by moving the gobo or trimming the branch.

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Use a hard, single source through gobos, blinds or foliage to cast graphic shadows across her form. Position the light carefully so pattern and skin balance, and expose to keep the shadow crisp and deliberate.

Model

Work with the shadow rather than against it, placing your face and body so the pattern falls where it flatters. Hold still once the light lands so the graphic edges stay sharp across the frame.

MUA & Hair

Keep skin matte and even so hard light and shadow read as clean form, not shine. Style hair with clear shape so it plays into the pattern rather than muddling the cast lines.

Stylist

Choose simple, smooth surfaces that let the projected pattern become the subject. Mind the heat and safety of a hard source close to set, and keep her clear of hot fixtures between takes.

Poses & body

  2. Hand raised into a hard beam, shadow cast on the wall

  4. Face behind a patterned gobo throwing lace shadow
  5. Reaching so the arm’s shadow extends the pose
  6. Seated with a shaft cutting across the eyes
  7. Fingers spread to fan shadow lines on the skin
  8. Turning so the shadow pattern slides over the face
  9. Peering out from a pool of shade into the light
  10. Body angled to lengthen a dramatic cast shadow
Expression & mimic
  • Mysterious calm within the striped light
  • Intense eyes catching the single lit band
  • Serene stillness half-lost in shadow
  • Moody downward gaze in the dark half
  • Quiet drama, lips relaxed
  • Direct gaze from the lit sliver of face
Directing cues
  • “Find the line of light and let it cross your eyes”
  • “Turn slow so the shadows slide over you”
  • “Lift your hand into the beam, watch the wall”
  • “Stay in the dark, just your eyes in the light”
  • “Hold there, the shadow is part of the pose”
  • “Lean into the light one inch, and freeze”
MUA & hair
  • Matte skin so hard light won’t blow out
  • Defined brows and eyes to hold in shadow
  • Sculpted cheekbones the raking light will carve
  • Sleek hair that keeps clean shadow edges
  • Bold lip to anchor the lit portion of the face

Vol. 99Creative · Long Exposure

Long Exposure — Motion & Trails

Long exposure lets one subject stay anchored while time smears everything else into motion. The craft is holding the person genuinely sharp with flash or bracing, then letting ambient and movement paint the rest.

AdvancedKit Tripod + creative tools
CreativeLong ExposureStill centreDragged shutterCity trails

RelatedShadow Play — Pattern & Form · Light Painting — Drawn Light · Double Exposure — Layered Frames

Baseline — Motion & Trails

Anchor

Freeze the subject with a flash pop or a braced, still pose.

Support

Tripod and remote release remove all camera shake.

Exposure

Stop down and add ND so ambient can build over seconds.

Capture

24mm f/11 · ISO 100 · 2-6s · ND filter, tripod.

Starting exposureManual / Bulb · 1/15 to 30s · f/8–f/11 · ISO 100 · tripodDarken the room and drag the shutter or open on Bulb. Lock the camera down, shoot many, and check the trails at 100%.
01
Still centre

Sharp Amid Motion

Keep the subject sharp while movement blurs around her.

Shutter
2-4s
Aperture
f/11
ISO
100
Flash
Freeze pop
ND
3-stop
A

Set & Instrument

Pose the subject in a stable, braced stance and let people or cloth move around her. A single flash pop pins her sharp while the open shutter records everything else as motion.

B

Lighting Micro-Adjustments

Balance flash to ambient so the frozen figure sits naturally inside the blur, not cut out from it. Feather the key to keep her separated from a busy background.

C

Read & Faults

Slight subject blur means she drifted; shorten the exposure or brace harder. If she looks pasted on, the flash overpowered ambient and needs dialling down.

02
Dragged shutter

Ambient Drag

Drag the shutter to swirl ambient light behind a lit subject.

Shutter
1/4-1s
Aperture
f/8
ISO
200
Flash
Rear-curtain
Move
Slight pan
A

Set & Instrument

Set a slow shutter and a small flash so ambient smears while the subject reads sharp. A gentle handheld pan turns background lights into soft ribbons of colour.

B

Lighting Micro-Adjustments

Use rear-curtain sync so the sharp exposure lands at the end of the drag and trails follow the motion. Keep flash modest so the ambient blur remains visible.

C

Read & Faults

Too much flash freezes everything and kills the effect; lower its power. A pan that is too fast turns lights to unreadable streaks, so ease the movement.

03
City trails

Streets & Streaks

Set a portrait against streaking city light trails.

Shutter
4-6s
Aperture
f/11
ISO
100
Flash
Freeze pop
Safety
Off roadway
A

Set & Instrument

Position the subject on a safe kerb or plaza where traffic passes behind, never in the roadway. Open a multi-second exposure so headlights draw trails while a flash pins the portrait.

B

Lighting Micro-Adjustments

Match flash colour to the street ambient with a warm gel so the figure belongs to the scene. Balance power so trails stay bright and the face is not overlit.

C

Read & Faults

Prioritise safety: keep the subject and gear clear of moving vehicles at all times. If the sky blows out, add ND or shorten the exposure and rely more on flash.

On-set crew brief
Photographer

Set a long exposure on a locked tripod so surrounding motion trails while she holds sharp at an anchor point. Balance ambient and a freezing flash so the trails glow without losing her clean edge.

Model

Stay perfectly still at the held moment so you render sharp while movement blurs around you. Breathe slowly and trust the count, since even a small shift softens the whole frame.

MUA & Hair

Build a look that stays crisp through a long, still frame and reads under the brief freezing light. Secure hair so no stray strand drifts and smears the sharp anchor of the shot.

Stylist

Dress in pieces that hold their line during the long hold yet let motion elements trail gracefully. Keep safety around the dim set and any moving light sources in mind, taping cables and clearing her footing.

Pose & direction library
Poses & body
  1. Seated rock-still as movement streaks around you
  2. Standing centred while a light trail sweeps past
  3. Profile held motionless against a blurred backdrop
  4. Arms folded, planted, sharp amid the smear
  5. Head resting on hand, frozen through the frame
  6. Facing a held light for a steady soft key
  7. Reclined and still as ambient streaks flow over
  8. Standing tall, one anchored contrapposto pose
  9. Chin lifted, eyes fixed, body a still point
  10. Back turned, silhouette crisp against moving light
Expression & mimic
  • Perfectly steady face for the slow shutter
  • Eyes locked and unblinking on one point
  • Serene closed eyes, no drift or flutter
  • Calm neutral jaw held for the exposure
  • Quiet contemplative gaze, fixed
  • Soft still half-smile that never moves
Directing cues
  • “Be the one still thing while the world blurs”
  • “Lock your eyes and hold, long shutter running”
  • “Slow shallow breaths, keep the shoulders quiet”
  • “Don’t blink till I count you out”
  • “Anchor down, let the light do the moving”
  • “Statue-still now, this frame takes its time”
MUA & hair
  • Fix hair firmly so no strand drifts and blurs
  • Slightly bolder makeup to read in low light
  • Add a subtle sheen to catch passing streaks
  • Set the base so it holds through a long frame
  • Define the eyes to stay sharp in the dim key

Vol. 100Craft · Business

The Business — Client Experience

A photography business is the sum of promises kept, from first enquiry to final print. Great images earn attention, but a clear offer, a calm session, and reliable delivery earn referrals.

IntermediateKit 1–2 lights + a modifier
CraftBusinessThe offerThe sessionDelivery

RelatedTethering, Colour & Workflow — The Bench · Business On-Location — The Workplace · Set Design & Backdrops — The Build

Baseline — Client Experience

Clarity

State what the client gets, when, and for how much, without ambiguity.

Comfort

A relaxed subject photographs better than a technically perfect setup.

Consistency

Deliver the same standard every time so trust compounds.

Capture

Workflow note: enquiry, contract and deposit, session, gallery, print order.

01
The offer

Tiers & Pricing

Package your work into clear, comparable options.

Tiers
Three
Anchor
Middle option
Deposit
Books the date
Contract
Signed first
Extras
Prints, album
A

The Offer

Offer three tiers so clients choose between options rather than whether to book at all. Design the middle tier as the one you want most people to pick, with the others framing its value.

B

The Experience

Send a short guide before booking so expectations on time, deliverables and price are set early. A signed contract and deposit protect both sides and turn interest into a firm commitment.

C

Delivery & Standards

State turnaround and image counts in writing so there is nothing to negotiate later. Price for the full workflow, not just shoot time, so editing and delivery are properly covered.

02
The session

Calm & Confident

Run a session that puts nervous clients at ease.

Start
Easy poses
Pace
Unhurried
Cues
Show, then guide
Music
Sets mood
Breaks
Reset & review
A

Set & Instrument

Open with simple, forgiving poses so a shy client sees quick wins on the back of the camera. Keep direction concrete, giving small physical cues rather than asking them to feel a mood.

B

Lighting Micro-Adjustments

Use a broad, soft key so people relax under flattering light and forgiving falloff. Adjust the light around the subject rather than asking them to hit precise marks.

C

Read & Faults

Tense shoulders and a fixed smile mean pull back and reset with conversation. Show one strong frame early, since seeing themselves look good unlocks genuine expression.

03
Delivery

Gallery & Print

Deliver galleries and prints to a consistent standard.

Gallery
Online proof
Retouch
Natural, consistent
Prints
Calibrated lab
Backup
Two locations
Delivery
Within promise
A

Set & Instrument

Present finished work in a clean online gallery that makes selecting and ordering prints simple. Curate to your best edit rather than dumping every frame, which protects the client experience.

B

Lighting Micro-Adjustments

Retouch to a natural, repeatable standard so skin and colour stay consistent across a set. Soft-proof and order from a calibrated lab so prints match what the client approved on screen.

C

Read & Faults

Deliver on or before the date you promised, since late galleries erode hard-won trust. Keep two backups of every job so a drive failure never becomes a client crisis.

On-set crew brief
Photographer

As studio owner, set the tone the client feels from first enquiry to final reveal, protecting a calm, confident experience at every step. Lead the vision and the room so each woman leaves feeling seen, celebrated and eager to return.

Client Care

Guide her through booking, preparation and the shoot day with warmth and clear communication so nothing feels uncertain. Anticipate nerves and needs, turning a photoshoot into a genuinely reassuring, personal occasion.

The Team

Move as one crew where stylist, artist and assistants each quietly elevate her comfort and confidence on set. Read the room together, handling the details so she only ever feels the ease, never the machinery.

Delivery

Retouch and present the gallery with taste and speed so the final images honour how she felt in the room. Package and hand over the work as a memorable finish that turns a happy client into a lasting advocate.

Pose & direction library
Client posing for shy clients
  1. Start seated and turned away, just glance back at me
  2. Rest both hands on a prop so they aren’t idle
  3. Look off to the window first, not the lens
  4. Cross one ankle behind the other to soften the stance
  5. Hold a warm drink and simply cradle it
  6. Walk slowly toward me while we chat, no posing
  7. Lean a shoulder on the wall and breathe out
  8. Tuck a strand of hair back, a natural small motion
  9. Sit sideways and turn only the head to camera
  10. Close your eyes, take a breath, open on my count
Confidence cues
  • Roll the shoulders back and down before each frame
  • Plant the weight on the back foot to feel grounded
  • Lengthen the neck to instantly look assured
  • Unclench the hands, keep the fingers soft
  • Find your best angle and return to it often
  • A slow exhale before the shutter melts the tension
What to say
  • “You’re doing brilliantly, this is already lovely”
  • “There’s no wrong move here, just be with me”
  • “Take a breath, we have all the time we need”
  • “That last one was gorgeous, want to see?”
  • “Forget the camera, just talk to me a moment”
  • “Shake it out, laugh it off, and let’s go again”
Prep & wardrobe advice
  • Bring two or three outfits in your true colours
  • Steam garments the night before, no last-minute creases
  • Choose pieces that fit now, not aspirationally
  • Keep prints simple so the eye stays on you
  • Pack a spare in case a look feels wrong on the day

Appendix A — Starter kit

What to buy first

You do not need everything at once. Each tier below runs most of this book; add pieces as your work grows.

Starter (one light)

  • One flash or strobe + a trigger
  • A softbox or shoot-through umbrella (85–120cm)
  • A 5-in-1 reflector (white / silver / black)
  • A light stand and a sandbag
  • One fast standard lens (35mm or 50mm)

Growing (two lights)

  • A second head for fill, rim, or background
  • A beauty dish or a grid for the key
  • A collapsible black flag / V-flat for negative fill
  • A seamless roll (white + grey)
  • A 24–70mm zoom and an 85mm for portraits

Pro (the full bench)

  • Three-plus heads, gels, grids, snoots, barn doors
  • Large scrims and a boom arm
  • Tether cable + a colour-checker chart
  • A macro lens for product and beauty detail
  • HSS-capable strobes for sun and freeze work

Appendix B — Templates & checklists

Reusable

Pre-shoot checklist

  • Brief agreed, references shared, shot list built
  • Batteries charged, cards formatted, gear tested
  • Wardrobe steamed, MUA & hair confirmed, call times set
  • Location scouted, permits / permissions where needed
  • Backup plan for weather or a no-show

Delivery checklist

  • Cull and rate; back up to two places before editing
  • Colour-correct to the chart; retouch to the genre standard
  • Export web + print sizes; sharpen for output
  • Deliver via gallery with clear usage terms
  • Archive the finals and the selects

Model release — essentials

  • Names and date; description of the shoot
  • Scope of use (portfolio, commercial, editorial, web)
  • Duration and territory of the licence
  • Signatures; a guardian signs for minors
  • This is a plain-language guide, not legal advice — have a lawyer review your final form.
